The House resumed from Friday, October 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take much time of the House, but I do wish to express my objections to the thrust of Bill C-55.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we were summoned in the midst of the summer recess in order that Parliament could deal with what the Government of the day deemed to be an emergency situation. That resulted from the fact that 174 Sikhs landed on the coast of Nova Scotia. Because of this particular matter, and the queue jumping the Government deemed to be in vogue at that point in time, it required us to return to Parliament. However, we have dealt with that particular Bill, but there are linkages to this particular piece of legislation, Bill C-55.
In my view, the thrust of the Government's legislation points out a number of serious weaknesses, for instance, the prescreening system, the safe third country concept, the refugee board, the appeal system, as well as the precedent that Canada has set for other countries encouraging them to consider similar action by turning a blind eye to the plight of refugees. The situation with regard to refugees ought to be clear to Canadians. We are a very fortunate country to have in our midst a large number of refugees from all over the world who have come to Canada and have become exemplary citizens for all Canadians to observe and, indeed, with whom to participate and interact.
With its obvious apparent weaknesses, this Bill ought not to pass Parliament. I wish to give credit to my colleague from Toronto who has led the charge in opposition to Bill C-55. He has set out very clearly and unequivocally the objections that he and other members of our Party have with regard to Bill C-55.
It is one issue when queue-jumping takes place and individuals jump ahead of the line who are not legitimate refugees. But the over-all Canadian policy which is now codified into law, particularly an appeal system which I and many lawyers and organizations in the community at large oppose for a variety of reasons, ought to be amended and amended very clearly in order that we can improve upon that system.
In summations, I am opposed to Bill C-55 for many of the reasons which have already been announced by my colleagues in the House. Upon reflection, I would hope that the Government would change this particular Bill in order to address the very serious errors and omissions which are tied into Bill C-55.

1 wish to emphasize the present reality. Since World War II Canada has received more than 400,000 refugees from other countries. Those people have made a signal contribution to the social, economic, and political life of Canada. In recognition of the work and attitude of Canadian people toward refugees, last year the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees presented the Canadian people with the Nansen Medal. This was a very signal honour for the Canadian people as a whole. The great majority of Canadian people support the admission of genuine refugees to Canada. They wish the abuses cleaned up, but they wish Canada to continue to receive people from other parts of the world who are in genuine need.
With Bill C-55 we are returning to some earlier attitudes. We are turning back the clock, because the present reality of openness was, of course, not always the reality in Canada. We do not need to go too far back in our history to find some pretty shocking and disgusting incidents of racism. There are situations where racism was not only an incident but was institutionalized in our laws. For example, the Oriental Exclusion Act provided that male workers from Asia could come to Canada to work, but they could not bring their families. This was a cruel type of legislation that helped to perpetuate many stereotypes about Asians. Some of those stereotypes still linger in the minds of some Canadians.
Because people from India were British subjects and hence eligible to come to Canada as immigrants, Canada took a very devious round-about way of excluding them. We passed an Order in Council which required that they come on a boat directly from India without stopping in a third country, when we knew very well that there were no direct passenger lines from India to Canada. It is the same kind of government subterfuge which we see in Bill C-55. The Order in Council eventually led to the Kamagata Maru incident when a boat was chartered to bring people directly from India to Vancouver, and Canadian racism erupted in a very ugly manner which eventually led to the death of a number of Sikhs.
I would like to give some examples of earlier racism. We know the sad story of the turning back of the St. Louis with Jewish refugees on board at the close of the 1930s. These people had no alternative, when Canada and other countries shut the door to them, but the Holocaust of Hitler's Europe.
We can look at the attitude exemplified by R. B. Bennett on June 7, 1928, when he was Leader of the Opposition and spoke about European immigrants in the House of Commons. He said:
-These people-have made excellent settlers; they have kept the law; they
have prospered and they are proud of Canada, but it cannot be that we must
draw upon them to shape our civilization.
That kind of racism was widespread at that time. I presume that my grandparents, and perhaps even my parents, supported that kind of statement, a statement which nobody in the House would support today.
Immigration Act, 1976
On May 1, 1947, Mackenzie King said the following in the House of Commons:
I wish to state quite definitely that, apart from the repeal of the Chinese Immigration Act and the revocation of order in council-regarding naturalization, the government has no intention of removing the existing regulations respecting Asiatic immigration unless and until alternative measures of effective control have been worked out-
We reject that kind of open racism in Canada today, although at that time Mackenzie King was probably speaking for a fairly broad cross-section of Canadian people.
I could look at the example of my own church, the United Church of Canada. By the time the Right Reverend Hugh McLeod gave his address as Moderator in 1962, I think the United Church had far surpassed him in its openness and its attitude. However, we see in his statement some of the regrettable attitudes which continue to linger in Canada. He spoke of what he considered to be "the disproportionate influx of Roman Catholics by immigration", and said the following:
Perhaps Roman Catholics have been the only eligible immigrants available in large numbers, and as people they are doubtless estimable and capable of greatly enriching our nation, but as members of a Church which everywhere favours the establishment of a monolithic infallible authority under Rome, they may herald and achieve the end of liberty as we have known it and as we deem it necessary for life. Some will say, "But it is different here", and to them I say, "How is it different here?"
Such statements today can only make members of the United Church embarrassed that that attitude was common within certain sectors of our church just 25 years ago. Of course, the Moderator of the United Church never spoke ex cathedra, but that is illustrative of a certain attitude.
There are people today who want to go back to that kind of attitude. On September 19, 1987 The Vancouver Sun quoted former B.C. Supreme Court Judge J. V. Clyne saying:
I'd not want to see us cease to be a white country.
Canada never has been a white country, and I do not think it ever will be. J. V. Clyne is living in some kind of racist imagination of his own which has nothing to do with the present reality of Canada or with the kind of vision of a Canada that we want.
We have a new reality in Canada which is ashamed of the racism of the past and is open to genuine refugees. At the same time it recognizes that there has been a change in the place of origin of most refugees. After the Second World War most of them came from Europe. Around the end of the 1970s and into the early 1980s they came from southeast Asia. Today, most of the refugees who are trying to come to Canada come from Central America.
Perhaps another element of reality at which we need to look is the administrative backlog that has been built up. There has been a lack of staff. The Department of Employment and Immigration simply did not have enough people on staff to handle in a rapid and efficient manner people who came and applied for refugee status, so there were delays. As a result of the delays, people would remain in Canada for a longer period of time than what would have been expected to process their

October 20, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
case. Because they could stay here for such a long period, they began to use the delays and to abuse the refugee policy. Of course Portuguese Jehovah's Witnesses making false claims of persecution is a predominant example of that. Jehovah's Witnesses themselves do not give any credence to the claims of persecution in Portugal.
There has been a number of studies of the administrative backlog and what needs to be done. The best known would be the study done by Rabbi Gunther Plaut. Standing committee recommendations called for a speedier process, but one which would continue to give people due process and would continue to give them the right to a hearing within Canada, the right to appeal, and so on.
Despite the recommendations of a number of committees, the Government refused to act, and the backlog continued to grow until today when it is estimated to be somewhere between 20,000 and 30,000 people who are backlogged, still waiting to find out their final refugee determination. Some of those people are genuine refugees; some of them are bogus refugees. However, the Government's refusal to act almost indicates that it wanted the crisis to develop.
1 want to suggest that Bill C-55 is not aimed primarily at the backlog or at the causes of the backlog. Bill C-55 is aimed at the perceived threat of an influx of refugee claimants from Central America via the United States. It is not aimed at bogus refugees, although it will weed out some of them, but it is aimed at genuine refugees who will also have a much more difficult time getting into Canada.
In one year Guatemala had some 400 people applying to Canada for refugee status. Some 75 per cent of these people were recognized as refugees. In fact, the repressive conditions in Guatemala and El Salvador have produced hundreds of thousands of refugees. Many of them have gone to Mexico where they must exist in absolutely deplorable conditions in refugee camps. Others have entered the United States as illegal aliens. United States policy has made it almost impossible for those people to achieve refugee status.
In 1982, some 12,000 Salvadorans applied for asylum in the United States, and only 26 were accepted. Something like .2 per cent of refugee applicants were accepted as refugees coming from El Salvador.
Last year, the United States passed legislation which provided for fines of $10,000 for anyone employing or harbouring illegal refugees. When they are caught in the United States they are returned to their country of origin. If the country happens to be El Salvador or Guatemala, the refugee returnees are liable to torture, disappearance, or death.
Up until this year, if those people came to Canada they could be given special ministerial permits and relatively quick entry. Then new regulations were published last spring that slammed Canadian doors. It eliminated the list of countries,
including El Salvador and Guatemala, to which we would not deport people. In January and February this year 2,300 Salvadorans and 600 Guatemalans came to Canada from the United States and together with about 1,000 Chileans who arrived by air they equalled two-thirds of the refugee claimants at that time.
Professor Reg Whitaker contrasts the difference between our shabby, mean-spirited treatment of Central American refugees with our fairly generous treatment of some 60,000 refugees from Southeast Asia in 1979-80.
Mr. Whitaker asks:
What is the difference between the enthusiastic support for refugees in 1979-1980 and the closed door of 1987? Is it economic conditions in Canada? Hardly: unemployment is not worse now than then, and inflation is a good deal lower. Nor can it be racism, for Asians were the most discriminated-against group of immigrants to Canada.
There is only one difference, but it speaks volumes about Canada's vaunted international generosity. The Vietnamese and Cambodians were fleeing Communist regimes recently installed following military victories over U.S. fire power. The Latin Americans are fleeing anti-Communist regimes sponsored by the U.S. Oppression is defined in terms of where the oppressors stand in relation to the Cold War-and woe to any refugees who find themselves on the wrong side of that divide.
If the motivation for Bill C-55 and the restrictive regulations published last spring are not racism, the Government at least is using racism as a tool to push this legislation through. We saw the phony crisis that erupted this spring over the boat people when 174 Sikhs waded ashore in Nova Scotia. Canadians should be asking which is worse, genuine racism or using racism as a tool? I suggest that this Government has been using racism as a tool to pass repressive legislation.
An Hon. IVlember: False.

There was a backlog, which the Government allowed to develop of some 20,000 to 30,000 people in the system and then suddenly when 174 people who happen to be Sikhs came ashore in Nova Scotia the Government discovered that it had a crisis. There were all kinds of inflammatory statements made by Members on that side of the House and members of the press who whipped up the situation.
False.

The Government called the House of Commons back into session to deal with what was perceived as a crisis. Bill C-84 was introduced. The Government attempted to get Bill C-55 passed in that mood of crisis although the Government had known of the backlog of some 20,000 to 30,000 people for a number of years. It is despicable the way the Government has handled the whole business of using 174 Sikhs to whip anti-refugee sentiment in Canada in order to get this Bill passed.
When the Government introduced it, every knowledgeable group-churches, bar associations and refugee assistance organizations-opposed it and detailed the problems with it. Instead of having a reasoned debate and attempting to make
October 20, 1987

reasoned and reasonable amendments, the Government has attempted to push the Bill through.
Bill C-55 is not the answer to the backlog problem. It hits out at the wrong people. The legislative committees on Bill C-55 and on Bill C-84 were forced to meet while one was being debated in the House. That put a tremendous amount of pressure upon the critics, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) for our Party and the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) for the Liberal Party. It was unfair to the critics and unfair to the witnesses who appeared before the committee who were trying to make their case. The Government attempted to force the legislation through with a hothouse atmosphere. Of course, it did not work.
Major concerns remain even after the Government introduced some minor amendments. These major concerns remain. As Ms. Kutz-Harder from the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees pointed out to the legislative committee:
A few minor amendments cannot rectify the fundamental flaws of the current Bill C-55.
We have reviewed the attempts by several groups to propose amendments which try to make sense of Bill C-55 and make it workable and just. However, clause by clause amendments cannot correct the fundamental flaws of the Bill.
We ask the Government to begin again in the face of a more just and more viable alternative. The most responsible action which this legislative committee could take would be to make the recommendation that the Government reconsider and replace this Bill with legislation consistent with the widely supported alternative procedure, which would better protect genuine refugees and certainly deter abuse.
In its present form, Bill C-55 still gives immigration officials the power to screen out refugee applicants before they get a chance to make their case to the refugee division. It still denies them the right to a proper appeal process.
I would like to close by giving the last word to Victor Velasquez, Vice-President of the Canadian Hispanic Congress who said:
We are convinced that the Bill worsens the situation of genuine refugees and makes protection for them almost inaccessible and practically illusory. We are facing an abuse psychosis and we are forgetting the universal values that we should maintain as human beings in dealing with other human beings who are fleeing from repression and death.
That is the reality of refugees in our world. Bill C-55 neglects that reality. It is trying to change the reality of Canada as being a relatively open decent society into being one of a closed door with a closed mentality.
I urge the Government to consider again whether it wants to enforce this kind of repressive reality upon Canada in 1987.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) and, in particular, his remarks about what has been called the Sikh boat load and his suggestion that the Government used the occasion of that to promote racism as fuel for this legislation to pass. I would like to ask the Member to comment on another aspect of that same situation.
Immigration Act, 1976
Throughout the year we have had growing suggestions associating refugee claimants with terrorism. There were a number of unfounded accusations. For example, Maclean's published that 33 of those people had criminal records. When the former chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), went on the air the day Bill C-84 was tabled, he made the astonishing statement that the Bill is not about refugees but security. He suggested that refugees are security risks or may well be.
In light of the fact that the RCMP then testified to our committee that in relation to the 11,000 people which the RCMP had to examine last year and up to August this year, having no regular visas, there was no evidence of a threat to Canada and that included the Tamil and the Sihks boats, would the Hon. Member comment on how he finds the public perception of the Government's words in cases like that relating terrorism to refugee claimants? Has this done any damage to the public acceptance of refugees?

Of course it has, Mr. Speaker. We need only to recall that the first person of the 174 from the boat load dealt with by the authorities before being released to the general public was the person with the highest profile and about whom the most questions were asked as to whether or not the individual might have some unsavory and possible terrorist connections. The Government zeroed in on the person with the highest profile first to get the maximum kind of-
You're imputing motives.
Yes, I am imputing motives. I think the motives of this Government are reprehensible and the Canadian people will judge it on those motives.

Mr. Speaker, 1 think that Canadians want a fair and reasonable system for dealing with refugees. I think Canadians want a system that is consistent with our international obligations and the Charter of Rights. Unfortunately, the Bill C-55 before us today, is not that kind of legislation.
Yes, we do have a problem with bogus refugees. We are very well aware of that problem. That problem has arisen because the system has broken down under the weight of paper, memos and files going back and forth. It is a lousy system and people who work in the system know it is a lousy system.
Many recommendations have been made to improve the system. Since it has broken down it has provided people an opportunity to take advantage of it, and there have been bogus refugee claims. The bogus claimants have felt safe to remain in Canada for a very long period of time under the current inefficient system while waiting for the processing of their bogus claims.

October 20, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
1 share the concerns of my constituents and the concerns of many Canadians who feel that radical change is needed. Nonetheless, I cannot support this Bill because it will not attack that problem. What it will attack is genuine refugees. I think we will have on our consciences, if this Bill passes, that some genuine refugees will be turned away and returned to countries which are not safe. They will then be sent back to their own countries which they fled in the first place. We have to keep in mind that this inhumane Bill means that some people will die and some people will be tortured.
In my riding, there are a large number of immigrants. Many people are trying to get relatives into Canada legitimately, using the proper channels, and it is very frustrating for them to see other people make bogus refugee claims. That is a perfectly proper concern. We would like to see improvements made in the processing of immigrants and certainly in the processing of family reunification cases. That would be fair and highly desirable, but having an unfair process for refugees does not help immigrants either. It simply creates bad feelings.
I am pleased to see in my own riding that refugees are a matter of concern. A number of local churches have supported refugees. There are local committees on refugees and local agencies, and churches have sponsored particular families. The Woodgreen Community Centre Red Door program and St. John's Presbyterian Church have sponsored refugee families. My own church, St. Barnabas, has recently sponsored a refugee family which is integrating very well, considering their situation of confusion and desperation until they can get their long-term problems sorted out. In the meantime they are being treated well as refugees and their needs are being looked after. The Judgment Centre for Social Faith and Responsibility deals with the refugee question and indeed has come up with a number of proposals for better ways to change our laws.
I would like a take a few moments to look at what happened to get us in the mess we are in and why we need to have a better system. Canada's present law, the 1976 Immigration Act, provides for a system for the examination of claimants and decisions by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. It is a very cumbersome process. It has broken down because the number of claimants increases faster than the number of staff members needed to deal with the cases, so a great backlog has developed. Once the backlog developed, people knew it would be a couple of years before their claims would be processed and they began to take advantage of that.
There are fraudulent immigration consultants offering services and charging very high fees to people wanting to make use of their services to get into Canada in the hope that they will be able to get themselves settled while they are moving slowly through this very cumbersome procedure. The case of the fraudulent Jehovah's Witnesses from Portugal certainly shocked people. Yet when this happened, did the Government do anything about it? It waited for months before it even acted. The Government delayed imposing a visa requirement for 14 months after the scam was discovered, and 3,500 bogus claimants apparently managed to make their way in.
The Government has only itself to blame for this great pile-up of bogus refugees. It has not acted promptly. The law does need revision. The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration tabled a report in 1985, as a result of a study. This report proposes a swift, fair system of refugee status determination. The report proposes that a refugee claimant be sent directly to a refugee board without immigration procedures first. The refugee board would consist of people who would be trained to recognize legitimate refugee claims and a decision would then be made by them.
The Government was required to reply to the report four months after it was submitted, but it has never replied comprehensively to the report. Instead of dealing with these quite reasonable recommendations, it brought in its own Bill C-55. This Bill, if it is passed, would send a refugee claimant first to an immigration inquiry to determine whether or not there is any reason not to remove him or her. The immigration adjudicator, a member of the refugee division at this inquiry, examines only for the criteria of eligibility and credibility. This means that he does not judge the merits of the refugee's case itself, but only whether the claimant could have been safe in another country through which he passed and whether he could be removed to that other country.
What is wrong with this, of course, is that there is no guarantee, if the person is deported to the safe country from which he came, that he will be able to stay in that country. Of course, the prime example of this is Latin American refugees who go first to the United States. The United States is deporting refugees to countries where there are reprisals, torture and the disappearance of persons. While the United States will not harm these people directly, it will deport them to a place that will. Canada would then be doing indirectly, by deporting to the United States, what in good conscience we could not do and what would be so clearly and flagrantly contrary to our international obligations as a member of the United Nations. We could not deport people directly to a country where they are being persecuted but some of those people will, by being deported, indirectly end up back in those countries.
The New Democrats very strenuously oppose Bill C-55. It does have a few good points which have been remarked upon by other speakers. But I want to focus my remarks on what is very wrong with this Bill and how it goes completely against the obligations we have undertaken under the United Nations Convention that requires that everyone be accorded the right to make a refugee claim.
The United Nations Charter of Human Rights says that every persecuted person has the right to seek the protection of another Government. The Supreme Court of Canada decision in the Singh case in April of 1985 said that on the basis of the Charter everyone physically in Canada who makes a refugee claim has the right to be heard in person by the body that will decide the merits of the case. This Bill would certainly go against the rationale of that decision. The Charter of Rights also guarantees the right of access to counsel and there is a
October 20, 1987

right of appeal implicit in Canadian law which may be defended on Charter grounds.
Bill C-55 provides the right to appeal on only the most narrow and technical grounds, and limits the right to counsel. Counsel may not be legal counsel or counsel of the person's choice; counsel may be appointed, which would certainly not fulfill the requirements of the Charter of Rights.
Many Canadians have raised objections to Bill C-55. The Catholic Bishops have very strongly asserted their opposition to the injustice of this Bill. They say:

The Bill presented to Canadians fails to abide by any of the principles we have always supported. It is also regressive as far as our international responsibilities are concerned. Furthermore, it is unfair to refugees and to other countries of first asylum that are already overburdened.

The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops called instead for legislation which would give all claimants access to a full, fair, and independent hearing with a meaningful appeal procedure which would deal with the substance, something which Bill C-55 does not do. The Conference notes that this is a departure from our international obligations and how unfair it is to send refugees back to the country from which they came directly to Canada because these countries themselves are often very overburdened with refugees. Canada is exporting a problem which we are certainly able to handle as a relatively well off and well organized country.
According to the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops there is a false premise that Bill C-55 will protect genuine refugees. It will not do that. They say that the preliminary hearing is no more than an elaborate mechanical screening. They note that the abuses which are alleged and are the pretext for Bill C-55 are entirely the result of delays in reforming the present system. The answer, therefore, is to reform the present system.
Finally, they state that they will resist with unflagging determination the concept that this compromise is just for refugees. Refugees are among the most powerless people in today's world. We all know that to be the case. They are exploited, oppressed and fearful. When they arrive they have to make decisions and have decisions made on their behalf at a time of acute stress for them.
Rabbi Gunther Plaut is very well known for his work on refugees. Ele is a Canadian, having come here as a refugee. He has called for humane refugee procedures which will respect our international obligations. In Heart of the Stranger, a report on refugees, he stated:
We have a Bill that was constructed by the Commission of Employment and Immigration and is brought forward as the will of the people .... This Bill has the wrong focus. It is not a Bill to determine refugee status primarily: it is a Bill on how to deport people primarily... . It is Filled with constitutional problems. The process it proposes is not shorter but longer.
Immigration Act, 1976
Unfortunately, all of that is true. All of these criticisms are perfectly correct and are shared by many Canadians; experts, voluntary groups, church groups, and many others who are concerned that Canada live up to its obligations.
The Jesuit Centre for Social Faith and Justice, which is based in my own riding but which, of course, has a mandate much beyond that, has come forward with many recommendations on how to deal with the situation and supports the previous Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration approach which was a much more humane and probably more efficient approach.
The first step that they propose is that the claimant be examined by an immigration officer and referred for inquiry. Second, there would be a hearing before a two-person board which would be held within two weeks and the decision would be immediate. This would cut through the problem of cases piling up for two or three years which makes it possible for bogus refugees to take advantage of the system. Third, if the person is refused he or she could apply for a review to a centralized review board. Again, a decision would be anticipated within weeks. Therefore, an appeal would be allowed but it would be a speedy procedure. Fourth, if the person's appeal was refused, the person could appeal on legal grounds to the Federal Court. There are only four steps. Everyone would get a hearing and it need not take a very long time.
The Jesuit Centre for Social Faith and Justice notes all of the problems associated with the lack of access to counsel. They note the problem, with which anyone who has worked with refugees is familiar, that the person needs a bit of time to find out what is happening. Genuine refugees are scared and upset when they arrive. They may be ill. They have all kinds of problems. In order to make such fundamental decisions they need time to talk to people, to establish trust, and to know whether the advice they are getting is reasonable.
These people have been abused by the authorities of their own countries. They need time to figure out what authority figures can be trusted and where they can get fair advice. The procedure proposed in this legislation does not allow for that. They would be put through the procedure without counsel of their own choice. They would have to make a claim instantly and would have to make decisions before they are properly prepared to do so.
If the credible basis test fails a person can be deported back to the country for which they feel persecution without a full hearing. What is the credible basis and how accurate are the Government's criteria? We know that the Government can make mistakes in these matters. We know that for a number of months Chile was not considered to be an unsafe country. Instead of looking at the person's actual situation there is an objective list. The list can be out of date and the person's circumstances may be different from those of other people. There is no provisions in Bill C-55 for examining the actual circumstances of an individual.

October 20, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
We need a crackdown on abuse. We want a better and more efficient system which works speedily, but it must have proper procedures for control as well. It must have proper appeal procedures, opportunity for counsel, et cetera.
I would like to say a little about the Government's approach to this issue. I am very concerned about the approach contained in Bills C-84 and C-55. This is Draconian and very cynical legislation. It foments bad feelings. At a time when we have unemployment and other difficulties the Government is taking a get-tough approach. With bogus refugees, ambiguous situations, and growing numbers of refugees the Government wants to get tough.
Only very recently Canada became humane in its refugee determination process. We have a sorry history in this regard. We have turned away Jews and Sihks who were persecuted when they returned to their countries. Frankly, we had a racist immigration policy until very recently which, of course, also affected the refugee process. However, Canada finally did sign and ratify the United Nations Convention on Refugees and has done some very good work on refugees. We accepted a large number of people from Southeast Asia and dealt with them in a very humane way.
In the meantime Canada has changed. With Bills C-55 and C-84 we are taking a big step backwards. Instead of building on Canada's recent steps toward being humane, generous, reasonable, and exercising our international obligations, we are going backwards. This is unfortunate.
1 call on the Government to live up to its commitments, to show leadership, and not be cynical. I call on it to reconsider and replace Bill C-55 with legislation that would be humane and just, in accord with our principles in the Charter and with the United Nations Convention.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot really say that I am glad to take part in this debate because this legislation is so poor that one would rather not see it before the House. However, I will share a few of my thoughts about the Bill.
In August the Government called Parliament back for an emergency session in order to deal with refugees. We are still here many weeks later dealing with legislation that I believe is politically motivated.
While we are dealing with two pieces of legislation concerning refugees, Bill C-55, which concerns the over-all refugee system, and Bill C-86 which deals more specifically dealing with people arriving here by boat with seeming impunity, we are essentially with one issue. That issue is the fairness of our immigration and refugee systems. The events which have occurred in the last while have caused Canadians to put in doubt our refugee and immigration systems. Many Canadians have the impression that the system is open to abuse because many have spent years trying to gain access to this country for
their relatives only to be frustrated in the majority of cases, and suddenly they see refugees getting on a boat and being able to come to Canada where the doors are open to them. People have felt that this is unfair and have demanded that the Government take the appropriate action.
The Government studied the situation and decided that this was a political opportunity to show Canadians that it was responding to their sentiments. Therefore, it drafted some very tough legislation and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that he would call back Parliament for an emergency sitting to deal with queue-jumping and the fact that so-called refugees were getting through an open door while the relatives of other Canadians could not get into Canada. According to parliamentary reform, the House is not supposed to sit during July and August. Yet, the Prime Minister disregarded this and announced that he was calling an emergency session of Parliament so that he could appear to be taking action and showing strong leadership.
It is interesting to note that the Government called back Parliament last summer as well, in a similar situation, choosing to serve its own political interests rather than respect parliamentary reform and follow the parliamentary calendar upon which we all agreed. Of course, the Government is taking every political opportunity it can, because it is so low in the polls it is afraid it will never regain its standing.
We are rapidly gaining.

I hear a faint echo that the Conservatives are rapidly gaining. It depends whose poll one reads.
It took the Prime Minister 10 days after his announcement to call the emergency session of Parliament. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) explained that the Prime Minister did not have time to write the appropriate letter. However, one would assume that an emergency session of Parliament is meant to deal with an emergency situation.
While the Prime Minister eventually found the time to write the letter in order to call back Parliament, summer has long since passed and the leaves are turning colour. It will not be long until we feel the cold winds of winter, yet we are still in an emergency session, presumably to deal with the emergency.
The fact is that we have dealt with many other pieces of legislation since we have returned. Furthermore, Question Period has functioned in the normal fashion, during which we have dealt with the issues that appear on the front page of The Globe and Mail. In other words, we have been proceeding with the normal day-to-day work of the House of Commons.
Was Meech Lake an emergency?

My colleagues asks whether the Meech Lake Accord is an emergency. We dealt with that question yesterday and will be dealing with it in the days to come. Obviously that question must be dealt with, but surely it is not an
October 20, 1987

emergency and not the reason that the Prime Minister called back the House of Commons.
When one considers the delay in calling back the House of Commons and the fact that the Government introduced other business that takes place in a normal session of Parliament, one must question whether the Government really called back Parliament in order to deal with an emergency. Rather, it raises the possibility that the Government was trying to take advantage of a political opportunity as a result of the hysteria and fear developing among Canadians because of the arrival of refugees to this country in boats operated by private contractors.
Clearly, the way this question has been handled in Parliament indicates that the only emergency was for the Government to take advantage of a political opportunity. I question whether the Government is dealing with an emergency when we are here going about the normal work of Parliament on a day-to-day basis.
Let me deal more specifically with Bill C-55.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: It is about time.

My colleague wants to hear about Bill C-55. I will certainly give him my analysis and hope that he will meet the challenge and speak to the Bill himself in order to explain his point of view.
Our Party believes that where the refugee system is being abused there is a need for change, but there are ways of changing the system that are fair. There is a need to take action with regard to the refugee determination system. Certainly the backlog which exists in the refugee determination system indicates that the system is not up to par and must be reformed. We support change in this area.
However, once again, rather than reforming the substance of the refugee determination system, rather than changing the system to bring about better results, it appears that the Government is grasping at straws, seeking to grab a political opportunity. The Government came in with heavy-handed legislation, with a sledge-hammer, and really sought to give the impression to Canadians that it is going to be tough on the abusers of the system. There is nothing wrong with being firm, in playing the tough guy role, but if one goes too far and puts at risk the possibility of genuine refugees coming into this country, people who are seeking a safe haven, then the Government itself begins to abuse the refugee determination system by using it for political purposes.
In effect, what the Government has done is said to the Canadian people, "We are going to be tough on abusers". In order to sustain that impression it has brought in legislation so sweeping in its implications that it has put in doubt the opportunity of people who are not abusers, but who are in genuine need of protection, of coming into this country. This is an important point.
Immigration Act, 1976
Canadians are a generous and compassionate people. For years they have had a reputation of being open to people from other parts of the world when there was a need. Canada is a nation of immigrants, for the most part. Canadians want to help other people who are in danger when it is possible. They want to help people whose lives are at risk. Obviously, they do not want someone coming along and telling a big story just to get into the country, someone who could not normally get into this country. That is not what we are talking about. We are talking about people who are in genuine danger, who are living in some of the countries in Latin America where their lives are at risk because of civil war, those who have decided they are no longer willing to put up with dictatorial regimes and have struggled to overthrow those regimes and, in the process of doing that, have put their lives at risk. These people must seek refuge elsewhere, a safe haven, and Canadians have provided that safe haven. We do not want the system to be abused. We want to be able to continue to offer a safe haven to people who need it.
This legislation allows the Government to play the tough guy. We do not mind if it wants to play the tough guy as long as it does not carry it so far that it actually begins to hurt people. The problem is that the Government has carried it too far. This legislation has a number of key faults, one of which is that people will not be accepted as refugees if they come here from a country that is considered to be a safe country. For example, there are people from a Central American country who are temporarily in the United States and want to come to Canada because the United States will not give them haven because of the attitude of its president, Ronald Reagan. This provision puts the safety of these people in doubt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Are you sure about that? Ask your neighbour if you are accurate.

I hear the heckling and I appreciate the effort to engage in debate. I would urge the Hon. Member to rise at the end of my comments and enter a full speech on the record-give us his wisdom. We will certainly listen. We are prepared to hear him out because we want the full light of debate to be put on this legislation.
What I am saying is that it is likely that a Canadian Government in establishing what are safe countries would consider the United States to be a safe country. It would certainly be surprising if a Canadian Government in its refugee legislation was to say that the United States was not a safe country. I think that would shock most ordinary Canadians. It might even have a diplomatic repercussion for Canada. Who knows, Ronald Reagan might even tear up the free trade deal and go off in a huff someplace, which would not be a bad thing.
It is likely that the United States would be considered a safe country, yet we know that for people coming from Central American countries, where the United States is involved in its civil conflict, the doors are not open. The American administration really does not consider those people to be refugees.

October 20, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Yet they are refugees in the international sense of the word, in the sense that their lives are in danger through political conflict in their own countries.
These people are in need of safe haven. They should be able to have an adequate hearing in this country, and if their case is genuine we can open our doors to them. This law is flawed and this is one of the specific ways in which it is flawed. Another flaw is that there is no assurance in this legislation that someone will in fact receive a hearing, that they will be able to tell their story, make their case and indicate the reasons why Canada should accept them as political refugees. There is no assurance that they will have such a hearing. In fact, this legislation has a provision under which many people would be screened out before they could even get to Canada to receive a proper hearing. This legislation is seriously flawed.
It is important to realize that Canadians not only are generous and compassionate when it comes to people needing refuge, we have an international reputation as being a fair and just country. This reputation has been muddied by the international critiques of this legislation. Agencies of the United Nations have said, "Hold it, Canada. This legislation looks like it is going to do harm to genuine refugees. It looks like it is unfair". When an international body such as the United Nations says to take another look at our legislation, the Government ought to do so.
In closing, 1 wish to say that we were recalled for an emergency session in order to deal with refugees and queue jumping. While we wish the abuses of the system to be eliminated, at the same time we wish Canada to maintain its tradition as a compassionate country that has an open door to people who are in genuine danger and who need a safe haven. This legislation fails to meet those criteria, or meet that test. This legislation gives us a black eye internationally. This legislation has not been brought in to reform the refugee system. The only conclusion I can come to is that it was brought in to bolster the political agenda of the Government, for it to take advantage of a political opportunity to play the tough-guy role on the national stage in order to bolster its Gallop and Angus Reid ratings.
Speak to the Bill.

An Hon. Member has stated "speak to the Bill". I invite the Hon. Member and his Conservative colleagues who are heckling me to rise in the House and speak to the Bill. We will listen to what they have to say. Let them rise and add to the discussions and debate on this Bill. These are important matters, and we have raised crucial questions on the fundamental fairness of this legislation, as have international bodies such as the United Nations. I challenge Conservative Members to rise in the House and refute what we have said. If they cannot refute it, withdraw the legislation.

The Hon. Member has referred to the public excitement and anger surrounding the arrival of the boat load of Sikhs in the summer. I am wondering if the Hon. Member can tell us the responses of the people in his own constituency, or in the parts of Winnipeg that he knows, both immediately in the first few days following that incident and since then. The reason I ask is that my own experience was that constituents in Spadina were not nearly as upset at the outset as we have been told in general, and furthermore when they had a chance to learn more about the facts of the case they were even less upset by the arrival of the boat load, but became more upset by the legislation.
I received plenty of phone calls, but they were mostly from people in constituencies represented by Conservative Members of Parliament. Certainly in some cases it was quite evident that they had been put up to it by their Conservative Member who claimed, quite falsely, that the NDP and the Liberals had blocked Bill C-55 in the spring. Of course that is ridiculous since we have only a quarter of the votes we could not do that. The Government had not even tried to have more than three hours of debate on the Bill.
I found that there was not nearly the spontaneous anger at the Sikh boat load, at least in my part of Toronto, that some people had claimed there was all over the country. I would be interested to know what the Hon. Member can tell us of the opinions, both during the summer and at this time, of the people in his riding; church people, non-church people, people with knowledge of those matters, or people who receive their information from the front page of the paper or from television.

I thank my colleague for his question. Clearly this legislation and the events that led up to it require sober reflection. Early in the summer many headlines and television newscasts focused upon the boat people, and the people who were coming into the country. I must say that that type of coverage caused concern, certainly in the short term. I think that the Government saw that. Of course, there was much more hullabaloo and excitement in the press than at the grass roots level. That is not to say that there were not individuals who were generally concerned. A lot of people who were concerned were immigrant people who felt that, after struggling themselves to get their relatives into Canada, it was not fair that someone should be able to come in the back door without getting into line.
I found that as I talked to people and as they became aware of the contents of the legislation, they agreed that the legislation should not be so Draconian that it closes out or puts at genuine risk the possibility of real refugees coming into the country. People wished the abuses dealt with, but they certainly did not want the Draconian type of legislation that the Government has brought in.
The people have also begun to see through the smokescreen of the Government that, while it has been seeking to focus their attention upon refugee abusers, it has done nothing on
October 20, 1987

the central concern of the people in my riding which is family reunification. The Government has done nothing to make it easier for people to bring their relatives to this country. That is where their genuine need lies, and what they wish to see the Government act upon. Even during the hottest moments of the discussion their concern was on family reunification because they were looking at it from a fairness point of view.
There are many people in my riding who follow refugee, immigration and justice matters on a regular basis, particularly people who are involved in the churches. They were shocked and outraged by the legislation. They were disgusted. I do not know the correct word to use to describe how they felt about this legislation. Clearly they were saying that the Government has gone too far. It has gone beyond what is acceptable to Canadians. It is fine for the Government to play politics, but when it goes as far as to bring in the type of legislation that we have in the House today, legislation which will make it doubtful that even genuine refugees can gain access to Canada, then they say that the Government has gone too far, it should back off, and reconsider what is being done.

I wish to follow up on that particular train of thought. I found that a great number of people were concerned about queue-jumping. Perhaps the Hon. Member can shed some light on this. My understanding is that the queue for refugee claimants is quite a different queue than the one for regular immigrants, family reunification, business, or commercial entrants. Therefore, even the refugees coming in on the boats were not actually displacing any person in a particular queue. I wonder if the Hon. Member would comment on that.

My colleague has raised an excellent point. It brings some facts to this discussion. The reality and the fact is that no one's place in the line to bring in a relative for family reunification was disturbed by the entry of refugees into this country. In fact, if I understand correctly the comments of my colleague, who is a critic in this area and whom I have heard speak on previous occasions, the line for refugees was not full. In other words, there was still room under the allocations. I would think the same thing would apply under family reunification.
The point is that there are two different lines, two different movie houses. Those people who were coming in as refugees did not in any way retard the entry of anyone's relative. That is not to deny the point that Canadians, particularly Canadians of immigrant origin attempting to get their family members into this country, are not having a hard time. It is like dealing with a brick wall.
The Government has made as much a mess of its family reunification program as it has of the refugee determination process. While it is playing politics on the backs of refugees and putting at risk genuine refugees, when it comes to family reunification the Government is being hard-nosed and is not demonstrating any generosity of spirit.
Immigration Act, 1976
Most Canadians would agree that preference should be given to the family or relatives wanting to join immigrants living in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Government brought the House back several months ago-it seems almost like a year ago but it cannot be that long-to deal with a refugee crisis. It claimed that the crisis would be dealt with on an emergency basis by Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act. Today we are talking about Bill C-55, which is also an Act to amend the Immigration Act.
The two Bills were supposed to deal with the so-called emergency. Bill C-84 was supposed to keep people offshore who wanted to get into Canada. It was supposed to keep the door locked. Bill C-55 was supposed to deal with immigrants who managed to land in Canada. The intent of the Bill was to deal with immigrants, refugees, or whoever got into Canada, and to establish ways in which to send such people back.
As I say, we have two pieces of legislation. One is intended to keep them offshore and the other is intended to send them back if they get into Canada. That seems to be the main intent of the two Bills.
We should be looking at what Canadians expect from this kind of legislation or from any Government that is dealing with people. That is what we are dealing with here. We are not dealing with something nebulous which came in from Mars or from anywhere else. We are dealing with people who inhabit and share the planet Earth with us. They expect compassion and knowledge of the situation from any Government dealing with people. They expect the Government to have a listening ear in terms of their concerns, complaints, and the conditions under which they survived and which sent them to us. They also expect such a Government to make judgment on the basis of what it hears with a certain amount of compassion.
Canadians would also expect a very logical approach in legislation which recognizes and understands the problem being solved or supposedly solved by the proposed legislation. They would expect sensibility or a lot of common sense in dealing with these situations and with people in such a way that it arrives at a logical answer to most questions.
Last, and perhaps most important, they expect a certain amount of sensitivity to the needs of the people who are trying to get into Canada. In many cases they have been forced out of their homelands or have found themselves to be in danger. It should also have sensitivity to the fact that if they are arriving at our shores they may not have the kind of documentation or the kind of attitude which we would think is particularly good.
If any of us found ourselves to be in a position where we had to impress someone so that we could remain in Canada, we would be under such pressure that we might say and do things that would not help us along. We would not be ready for the kind of pressure put upon us and, consequently, the pressure would expand and have a real effect on us.

October 20, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
The Bills, the Government, and the bureaucrats should be sensitive to these facts. However, neither Bill C-84 nor Bill C-55 take into consideration any of the things we would expect in legislation dealing with people. It is not legislation which deals with money or property; it is legislation which deals with people, fellow inhabitants of this planet. We do not find compassion, logical approaches to the problems, common sense or sensible solutions, or sensitivity to the needs of people in these Bills.
Although Bill C-55 may have some very good points in terms of dealing with the problems which all of us recognize, it does not fulfill the expectations of people in terms of dealing with immigrants and refugees.
For years Canada has had a policy of welcoming immigrants and refugees according to processes established by law. These procedures were intended to limit abuse of the laws so that there would be no interference with the proper acceptance of immigrants and refugees. We in the New Democratic Party- and particularly our critic who has spent much time on it- know that the system broke down because too many people were coming into Canada. We also know that there was a need to change it and that it broke down because there were changes in the world structure. Refugees were being produced around the world at a much greater rate than we had ever seen before. Also, refugees who had been going to other parts of the world, such as Europe and Third World countries to a great extent, were not being accepted any longer. As well, because of economic situations and starvation in other parts of the world refugees were being created faster than other parts of the world could accept them.
It is interesting to look at the kind of situation which creates refugees or at the number of refugees which are being created every day. In the eyes of the Government, and in the eyes of many people, 174 people landing off the shores of Nova Scotia constituted a crisis about which something had to be done. It resulted in Bill C-84, and Bill C-55 which had been introduced earlier.
1 think it is important to put before the House and before the people of Canada the fact that every day for 365 days per year for the last 30 years an average of 700 people have become refugees. These figures are important to know. For instance, today in Central America there are one and a half million refugees. There are two million Palestinian refugees in the Middle East, and some of those refugees from Israel, the Gaza Strip or Jordan are second and third generation. Three million Afghans have fled to Pakistan and Iran since the Russians invaded Afghanistan in 1979. Some two million people were displaced in Vietnam, Kampuchea and Laos over the last 10 years. In 1980 to 1985 some 400,000 people were forced to flee from Uganda. Millions of Africans have been displaced by war, internal oppression, famine and ecological disasters, such as the advance of the Sahel.
All of these are ways in which people become refugees and we think here in Canada-one of the richest countries in the world if not the richest-that when 174 refugees land off the coast of Nova Scotia that constitutes a crisis which requires Draconian legislation to ensure that it does not happen again. Compare the 174 refugees in Canada to the 400,000 who have been forced into refugee status by the famine in Africa.
Where are these millions of refugees going about whom 1 have spoken? Some of them are coming here but most are going to Third World countries. The average income of the inhabitants of those Third World countries is about $700 a year. I think that should give us a pretty good idea of what kind of a crisis there is with immigration and refugees in Canada. The basis of the Government's reaction to it should be looked at very closely. Can it be considered anywhere near a crisis? Obviously not.
If you were living in Malaysia over the last 10 years, Mr. Speaker, you would have expected 20 times as many boat people to land on those shores or on the shores of Hong Kong, if they could get that far, or on any islands surrounding that area. Every day in the summer 20 times as many as the 174 who landed in Nova Scotia land in Malaysia. If we have a crisis, then their crisis must be devastating.
Our Government decided, however, that there was a crisis and we would have to shut the doors as quickly as possible. As far as I know, no Canadian, outside of this Parliament possibly, has ever suggested that we leave the doors absolutely open to refugees and immigrants. Canadians have suggested some kind of control. That control has been set up and it has worked fairly well.
I know the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) talked about the slowness of family reunification which has been a problem. But still that aspect of immigration has moved along. A certain number have been allowed each year, but the process is slow and needs to be improved.
No one is suggesting that we shut the doors entirely. We are suggesting that we look at the existing structure, what is the Immigration Act, what is being supposedly amended and improved by Bills C-55 and C-84. We should find out whether they actually do what is intended to be done. We find that even as certain objectives and recognition of responsibility are stated as far as Canada is concerned, those two Bills, Bill C-55 in particular, do not do what those objectives say they should.
I think I should spend a little of my time looking at the real faults, recognizing that the Government tried, and we appreciate that, to improve Bill C-55. Unfortunately, the concerns that we, the church groups and immigration groups had back in May when the Bill was before the House still remain. The Government has not dealt with them. The Government used the 174 refugees arriving off the shores of Nova Scotia as a reason to bring Bill C-55 into the emergency session practically unchanged. The Government did not deal with the concerns
October 20, 1987

expressed by churches, refugee groups, lawyers and people helping refugees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: That is not accurate.

The Government did not change the Bill enough to alleviate those concerns. The shortcomings are still in the Bill. I suppose we could go over many of the faults in the Bill. First, the one that concerned most people last spring was the denial of the right to be heard. That position was not dealt with in Bill C-55. Nor is it in the changes to the Bill. I know that during 44.5 hours of testimony most people addressed the issue of the right to be heard, but did they not change the position of the Government. Consequently, the situation was not changed.
The UN covenant and protocol relating to the status of refugees signed by Canada in 1967 in Article 33 states that no country shall expel or return a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories when his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular group or social opinion. The recognized logic of this is that Canada has solemnly agreed that no one who is inside our borders who claims to be a refugee will be shipped out unless and until Canada has decided that the person's claim is unfounded.
We are now setting up a situation which makes it impossible for many people who would claim refugee status in Canada to be heard by the Canadian people. These two Bills will send them away as they come offshore or as they enter the country, even if they have not had an opportunity to be heard. In doing so, we are in contravention of the Convention because this violates Article 33.
Those are the kinds of things which have made me, other members of my Party and members of the public decide that this Bill should be withdrawn to allow us the opportunity to make the kind of changes that will make the system compassionate and humane.

I have just answered some correspondence from residents of my riding and I have a letter here from a Mr. David Bergen of Langside Street in Winnipeg. Fie takes aim at the Government on a number of issues and says:
-the issue which is uppermost in my mind right now ... is the Government's anti-refugee and anti-immigration attitude. I feel that the Tories are using the recent arrival of Sikh boat people to stir up racial prejudice and to provide a pretext for closing the door to thousands of legitimate refugees whom Canada is duty bound to accept under the United Nations accord. I fear that Bill C-55 (or the new version of it that the Government seems in such a hurry to get passed) will result in the exclusion of large numbers of people fleeing persecution, especially those refugees fleeing from El Salvador and Guatemala. Most of these refugees have no choice but to pass through the U.S. on their way to Canada, but under the new legislation they would be deported because the U.S. is a "safe country"-ignoring the fact that Salvadoran and other Central American refugees are being deported from the U.S. because the American Government does not acknowledge that a human rights problem exists in those countries whose governments it is propping up.
Immigration Act, 1976
I also note that the American Civil Liberties Union has found at least 50 cases of people who have been returned to their countries of origin from the United States being killed in El Salvador and neighbouring countries.
I wonder if my colleague would like to comment on the concerns my constituent raised about this legislation. It sure does not sound like the attitude the Government thinks all Canadians have with regard to the refugee determination process.

Mr. Speaker, the denial of the rights of refugee claimants to be heard means that they will be shipped offshore before they are heard. The first test of whether or not they shall be accepted and heard in Canada is the determination that they may have come through what are considered to be a safe third countries. That is what concerns the constituent who wrote to the Hon. Member.
The decision of whether or not a country is a safe third country is done mechanically. The bureaucrats look at a list of countries that are considered to be safe third countries, countries which comply with Article 33 of the Convention. But there have been cases of persons being rejected at Canada's border, sent back to the States and then sent from the States back to their country of origin and there have disappeared. The fact that a country says it complies with Article 33 does not necessarily mean that it does.
This test sounds like a good idea at first, but if we refuse to hear the refugee's story, we do not know whether the third country will be safe for him or whether it will ship him back to his country of origin where he will be persecuted or even killed. The concern raised by the Hon. Member's constituent is a concern which many people have had, and was one of the concerns of the churches, the refugees groups and the law reform groups that dealt with this Act back in its early stages. The safe third country concept does not become a direct violation of the Convention-it is an indirect violation.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to refugees in Africa. I know he is one of the few Members of this House who have some direct knowledge of Africa. I wonder if he could give us his opinion on whether the millions of refugees in Africa all wish to, would have the means or would intend to come to Canada, and if not, what he thinks is their future and what he thinks are Canada's obligations.

Mr. Speaker, I spent four years in northern Nigeria on the very borders of the Sahel. During that period of time we dealt with starvation and famine in the countries of northern Nigeria, Chad, and Niger. Canada has an excellent record of assistance in those countries. However, those people do not want to go anywhere but back to their land. They have no intention of being refugees in any other country but a place where they can wait out the period of time necessary for the situation to change enough that they can live in their own home countries. There is no doubt that we have a responsibility not only to feed them and to make sure they survive, but also

October 20, 1987
to make arrangements which will allow them to move to where they want to live.
