subsubtopic: INVITATION TO QUEBEC PREMIER TO REJECT FREE TRADE AGREEMENT UNTIL GOVERNMENT TAKES MEASURES TO PROTECT VICTIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 5 this year, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) admitted there would be losers, that some workers would lose their jobs as a result of the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States.
The same day, an economist at the University of Montreal published a study revealing that Montreal would lose 10,000 jobs in the short term as a result of free trade. Today, a study ordered by the Canadian-American Group sponsored by the C.D. Howe Institute recommends setting up programs to help the victims of free trade. Furthermore, all the experts admit that workers in the textile, footwear, clothing, shipbuilding and railway transportation industries will be severely affected.
Mr. Speaker, before anyone ratifies this Free Trade Agreement, we should first consider the potential victims.
All Conservative Members in this House should force the Government to set up retraining programs ... in fact, older workers will be the worst off because the Government has cut the early retirement program that was coupled with unemployment insurance, and we know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is discriminating against older workers with respect to unemployment insurance benefits.
I urge the Premier of Quebec to refuse to consider the Free Trade Agreement unless the federal Government takes steps to protect workers who are potential victims of this Agreement.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great sense of satisfaction and pride that I note the tremendous reception the people of Saskatchewan have given to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth.
Although my ancestry is not related to the Commonwealth and I am but a first generation Canadian, I am proud to be a loyal subject of so great and regal a monarch and pleased that the people of Saskatchewan have been so gracious to her. Therefore, I am astonished to learn of a faction in Canada committed to eliminating any mention of the sovereign in a proposed new citizenship oath. That means new citizens would not swear loyalty to the Queen but to the Constitution. Somehow that does not seem right.
There has been so much talk of late about maintaining our sovereignty and differentiating ourselves from our neighbours to the south; what better way is there than belonging to a Commonwealth and respecting an allegiance to a monarch? The Queen's loyalty to Canada has been unswerving.
Three cheers for the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) who assured the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), indeed all Canadians, that it is not the Government's intention to withdraw the reference to Her Majesty from the Oath of Allegiance.

Mr. Speaker, this week Ottawa is host to the Vice-President of Nicaragua, Mr. Ramirez. Many Canadians hope that the Canadian Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in particular will use this visit as an opportunity to show the same independence from the policies of Ronald Reagan that he showed in Vancouver from the policies of Margaret Thatcher.
We hope that in the discussions with the Vice-President of Nicaragua this week Canada will be able to consider what it can do in its own judgment and on its own merits, and not have to look south for tacit approval, to use an expression from a newspaper article today, in responding, for example, to a request by Nicaragua that Canada participate in a peacekeeping force, or whatever the request of the five Central American countries might be. This should be an occasion for the Prime Minister to show that Canada has an independent foreign policy not just with respect to South Africa and our former colonial master Great Britain, but with respect to Central America and our current colonial master, particularly since 1984, the United States of America.
October 20, 1987

subtopic: RED SWASTIKA PAINTED ON CANADA POST PROPERTY
RED SWASTIKA PAINTED ON CANADA POST PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first read the story which appeared in The Edmonton Sun last Sunday indicating that Dave Werner, President of the Alberta Federation of Labour, had painted a large swastika on Canada Post property, I was angry. This, 1 thought, is an insult to every veteran in Canada who fought against Nazism, and for a democratic Government that reflects the thinking of the people by doing things such as keeping the mail moving so small business and the rank and file would not be inconvenienced, and workers would be properly compensated for their work.
Then 1 read the story again. Behold, it was not a black swastika, the symbol of Nazism, but a red swastika, the symbol of the virtues of the heart; life, happiness, and good fortune.
Certainly defacing public property was an act of vandalism and the President of that Federation should have outgrown such a juvenile act, but as long as the red swastika remains on that fence it will say to Canada Post: "From the heart; good luck, good fortune and happiness!" I now wonder, because of this grievous error, will the NDP cancel his membership?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REBUILDING OF SAINTE-ANNE RIVER BRIDGE
REQUEST FOR REBUILDING OF SAINTE-ANNE RIVER BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a decision that will have a serious impact on the economy of the regions of Mauricie, Portneuf and Quebec City was made last August by Canadian Pacific.
The company confirmed it did not intend to rebuild the bridge over the Sainte-Anne River that was swept away by a combination of ice and spring floods last April. It explained that a study had been ordered and the results would be forthcoming in two or three years' time. This is a deplorable excuse. Meanwhile, at a time when VIA Rail is doing so much to improve the quality of its service, millions of dollars are being spent to build intermodal stations in Quebec City and Trois-Rivieres.
Canadian Pacific's decision is unacceptable in more ways than one, and it proves that the company has failed to consider the well-being of the community, since the decision is a threat to the economic development of the entire North Shore between Quebec City and Montreal.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Minister responsible for the Canadian Transport Commission, which has every authority over CP, to take the necessary action to have the railway bridge at Saint-Anne de la Perade rebuilt.
1 also want to express my support for colleagues in neigbour-ing ridings who are trying to get rail passenger traffic on the North Shore between Montreal and Quebec City restored as quickly as possible.

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF WORK OF CONSTABLE FUDGE
RECOGNITION OF WORK OF CONSTABLE FUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all know that the red-coated Mountie is probably the best known and most internationally recognized symbol of Canada. Over the past 114 years the RCMP has acquired a world-wide reputation for excellence, and legends surrounding the force have sprung up, many, if not most, originating in the Canadian North.
Recently the arrest of American fugitive Charles McVey by Corporal Dan Fudge of RCMP Teslin Detachment, Yukon Territory, has again given the force international prominence and perhaps added another northern legend.
As a result of his actions, the Government of the United States recognized him with two presentations. On October 15, 1987, Corporal Fudge was presented with the Outstanding Public Service Medal at the Pentagon by the U.S. Department of Defence. The following day he and another member of the force, Constable Vander Leek, received a citation from the U.S. Customs Service.
I believe we can proudly applaud the excellent work of this unassuming and obviously dedicated young man and rightfully claim that the stuff of legend can still be found under that Canadian symbol, the Mountie uniform.

Mr. Speaker, Our Common Future, the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, is currently being debated at the United Nations. This is a landmark, even revolutionary, report in the significance of its rethinking of the issues of the environment and economic development.
It is a report with hope also. It argues both for economic growth and the active combating of poverty, especially in Third World countries, along with concern for sustainable development.

October 20, 1987

The Brundtland Report promotes an intertwining of economic and environmental concerns in all stages of planning. It calls on us all, especially in industrial countries, to change our ways, to produce more with less, to develop renewable sources of energy, to change our positions on international development to assist other countries to reach sustainable development as well, and to change our policies with respect to our native peoples. We must consider the real costs of environmental pollution and ensure that it becomes cheaper not to pollute than to pollute.
This is not the time for pious statements about the Brundtland Report. It is a time for a serious rethinking of our ways. This report will require serious study and I hope it will receive it in this House soon. We need social and political change. We can and must do it for "our common future".

subtopic: U S S R.-PLIGHT OF YURI SHUKHEVYCH
U S S R.-PLIGHT OF YURI SHUKHEVYCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Yuri Shukhevych has spent 33 years in Soviet labour camps, prisons, and internal exile. He was first arrested as a 15-year-old boy and sentenced to 10 years imprisonment for the crime of being the son of the Commander in Chief of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. After serving the original 10-year sentence Yuri was re-arrested in 1958 for his continued refusals to condemn or renounce his father.
Shukhevych's plight has earned him the title of "The Eternal Prisoner". After years of imprisonment his health has suffered greatly. In 1980 part of his stomach had to be removed, followed by operations for cataracts and detached retinas in 1982. He has lost 99 per cent of his vision.
Shukhevych's plight is a warning to us all. As long as the Soviet Government continues to violate the fundamental human rights of its own citizens, the western nations must continue to view the so-called policy of "glasnost" with suspicion. I call on the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Government of Canada to use all of the resources at their disposal to effect the immediate release of Yuri Shukhevych and to send a clear reminder to the Soviet Government of its obligations as a signatory of the Helsinki Accords.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PREMIER
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my dismay over the comments of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) as reported in The Globe and Mail on October 17, 1987. Apparently the Deputy Prime Minister is upset with the Premier of Prince Edward Island who stated that the energy provisions of the free trade deal were not discussed at the Premiers' briefing.
The Deputy Prime Minister disagrees with Premier Ghiz and he is reported to have said: "Perhaps Mr. Ghiz was more interested in discussing potatoes." I want to remind the Hon. Member that our potato industry is very important, but we are also deeply concerned about our future energy supplies.
The consumers on our Island already pay the highest electricity rates in Canada. I believe that the Premier of Prince Edward Island expressed his genuine concern and I am disappointed that the Hon. Member for Vegreville would make this condescending remark. I am surprised that he would insult all those who are in our potato industry. Surely the Deputy Prime Minister now realizes that insulting Canadians will only make this free trade sell-out look even worse.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIF1CATION OF SOCIALIST PARTY'S DEMOCRACY

Mr. Speaker, throughout the world, socialist parties are totalitarian and centralist. However, when they see it is to their political advantage, they try and adapt to local custom. In Quebec, they do not use the same vocabulary they use for the rest of Canada. But how different is it?
The socialist leader should explain to the House why his only elected Member in Quebec slammed the door at his Party's meeting in Quebec.
Where is the democratic process in this Party? How come the Director of the Centrale de l'enseignement du Quebec, Mr. Michel Agnaieff, has more clout than the entire Quebec Socialist Caucus? October 20, 1987



Oral Questions

subtopic: LOW LEVEL OF TAX PAID BY CORPORATIONS
LOW LEVEL OF TAX PAID BY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, average Canadian taxpayers are fed up. They are fed up with a tax system that allows 80,000 corporations with profits of well over $10 billion to escape paying a single cent in tax, while many more only pay a small token fee.
Average taxpayers are wondering why Edper Investments Limited, a holding company controlled by multi-millionaires Edward and Peter Bronfman, paid just $6,000 in taxes in 1986, despite enjoying after tax profits of $207 million.
Average Canadian taxpayers are asking why the Bronfman brothers, estimated to be worth over $650 million, are paying less in tax than they are. Canadians are fed up with this unfairness. They have had it with the Government's tolerating and indeed contributing to it in budget after budget. They are as mad as hell and you can bet that they won't take it any more.

maintopic: OPPOSITION TO CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
OPPOSITION TO CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, free trade to this Government is alleged to mean that we as Canadians get access to the American market, but in fact the Americans get us and our economy for free. That is right, Mr. Speaker. According to the President of the United States, this trade agreement puts Canada in a continental union with the United States.
Clearly this is not in the best interests of a united, strong Canada. Realistically it is not surprising, given the Government's record and the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) obsession with pleasing the Americans.
On March 13, 1986, the Prime Minister said: "We will spare no effort to secure our access to the U.S. market". Well, he certainly spared nothing and he gave away our economic sovereignty in so doing. But the good news is that this deal can still be stopped. The United States must continue to be our most important trading partner, but we must not try to buy our way into one major market at the price of our sovereignty as the Government of Canada has done in this proposed free trade arrangement with the United States.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF MANITOBA PREMIER
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF MANITOBA PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an article appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on October 9, entitled "Does Pawley speak for Manitoba or the NDP?"
It accurately points out that in 1985 Premier Pawley not only advocated free trade with the United States but the creation of a common market. Premier Pawley said that he would support free trade: "as long as we preserve existing jobs, through a program of transition and analysis and at the same time obtain a guarantee to an access to future markets." That is exactly what our Government has achieved.
Now what has happened to Mr. Pawley? The federal NDP Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), and their Vice-President, Bob White, must have got to him.
Everyone knows the NDP support free trade and foreign investment, but only in Oshawa.
Premier Pawley's logic to support free trade in 1985 still exists today. Mr. Pawley's slogan in the last election was: "Standing up for Manitobans", but for whom is he standing up now? The federal NDP? He must stop being controlled by the big unions and their leaders in Oshawa.
Let us give Manitobans the opportunity to realize the benefits of free trade.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the stockmarkets around the world declined by a record amount. The Dow Jones fell by 500 points and the Toronto Stock Exchange fell by more than 400 points. Similar things happened in the Montreal Stock Exchange.
At 2.03 p.m., just before I came into the House, the Toronto Stock Exchange had fallen by an additional 333 points. That is 733 points in two days.
However, if we can judge by the Minister's answers in the House yesterday, he does not think the situation is too serious. Yesterday in reply to a question the Minister said:
I think the Leader of the Opposition is exaggerating in his reference to this morning's activities on the markets.
The Minister then went on to say-
Order.
Question.

-and I quote: "There have been some corrections in the financial markets". With the situation

October 20, 1987
Oral Questions
deteriorating by the hour on Canadian stock exchanges, does the Minister still believe that only "some corrections" have taken place in the stockmarkets which do not require any government action? Or has he finally realized, like all Canadians, that this is a major crisis which requires more than the Minister's passing interest as he watches from the sidelines as the world passes by?

Mr. Speaker, let me respond to the Hon. Member's question by saying the Government has taken some action. As 1 indicated earlier today I have spoken to most of my colleagues in the G-7 countries and there appears to be a broadly agreed point of view that we should be doing what we can to stabilize markets by ensuring that there is an adequate degree of liquidity in the financial markets. This has been done in Canada. For example, the Bank of Canada has acted accordingly.
The result has been a drop in interest rates in this country and other countries as well. I think this will contribute to achieving a greater degree of stability in the stock exchange markets.
However, 1 think we should be careful to understand that the stock exchange markets are the markets that have been the volatile ones. The bond markets, the interest rate markets, the foreign exchange markets, have been relatively stable during this period.

Mr. Speaker, it was clear to all Canadians, except, of course, the Minister of Finance, that there was a very serious situation developing in the stockmarkets of Canada and the world. I suggested to the Minister that some action be taken in terms of interest rates. This is exactly what he announced he has done today.
What prompted the Minister to abandon his laissez-faire policy of yesterday? Was he overruled by the Cabinet?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think this is the time to use these sorts of partisan jibes. I have indicated very clearly what I believe is necessary for achieving greater stability in the markets.
I have indicated to the House, as well as outside, that the underlying economies of Canada and the other G-7 countries are performing quite well. We reviewed this at the G-7 meeting in Washington toward the end of September, and that was the conclusion that we arrived at.
What we have seen is a major decline in stock markets. But I should draw the Hon. Member's attention to the fact that the Canadian market is below what it was at the beginning of this year, but not that far below what it was this year. The point I am making is that there was a substantial run-up in the market during the course of 1987. This has been taken away as a
result of the decline, but the underlying economies are still very strong.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister referred to the good performance of our economy. Granted, but I may remind him that those are the same comments President Hoover made in 1929. He even went to a baseball game to show that everything was o.k.
Oh, oh!
It is a historical fact. It's absolutely true.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF MORNING DECISION
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF MORNING DECISION
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister whether the decision he announced this morning to establish greater liquidity in the financial markets was made after consultation with members of the Group of Seven or did Canada act on its own in this case?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF MORNING DECISION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said in my answer that the decision that the Bank of Canada made today was based on consultations with my colleagues in the Group of Seven and consultations by the Governor of the Bank of Canada with other countries. I think the decision to provide for increased liquidity in the financial markets will help stabilize the market. I think we should understand that the present lack of stability is in the stock market, not in the financial or exchange markets.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Finance a question which I am sure is on the minds of millions of Canadians today in light of the worldwide stock market crash. The question is the following.
What is the Government doing, and what will it be doing to prevent this world-wide stock market crash from leading to a serious economic downturn, or worse, right here in Canada? Can the Minister gives us a clear and detailed answer, not only in terms of current action, but what it will be doing in the future?

Mr. Speaker, I have indicated what we are doing in the markets today through the Bank of Canada, and I think that this is having the desired result. We have seen a substantial drop in short-term interest rates where the bank rate, if it were to be set today, would probably be down three-quarters of 1 per cent.
The House Leader of the Liberal Party is asking what might we do in the future. It is important to realize that the underlying economies-the real economies as opposed to the stock market-in Canada, in the United States, and in other major industrialized countries are operating quite effectively.
October 20, 1987

If there is a need for further policy responses as things develop in the weeks or months ahead, we can review that at the time. I do not think it is appropriate to jump to conclusions on the basis of one day's understanding of a major decline in the market which took place yesterday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, the Minister speaks of one day, but it was some day!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the experts said that the world-wide decline on the stock markets wiped out $3 billion worth of securities held by Canadian pension funds on which millions of Canadian workers depend for a safe and secure retirement.
I want to ask the Minister what the Government will do to restore and safeguard the value of these pension funds, to give Canadian workers the assurance of a safe and secure retirement. Could the Minister give us a concrete answer today?

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Hon. Member has raised this point. I think Canadians should understand a few things about the state of their pension funds.
One is that there has been a significant increase in stock market prices over the last number of years. As I pointed out earlier, the current level of the Toronto Stock Exchange is what it was toward the latter part of last year, so that we have not lost a major amount in the longer term perspective.
The second and I think more important point is that the large majority of the assets in these pension funds are invested in bonds and in real estate. Both these markets have not been affected by the drop in the stock market. In fact, as I have indicated, the bond market has been up quite significantly and that should result in good profits for pension funds in that part of their investments.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MEETING OF GROUP OF SEVEN
REQUEST FOR MEETING OF GROUP OF SEVEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
The Minister said that he contacted the Group of Seven. He also said the crisis was a one-day crisis. The Minister knows perfectly well that the crisis is continuing today as well. It is world-wide.
In this context, is the Minister prepared to ask for a meeting of the Group of Seven?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MEETING OF GROUP OF SEVEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important to realize that my colleagues and I have had many consultations with the Group of Seven, and
Oral Questions
that we, like the other countries, have taken steps to deal with the situation here in Canada. The Governor of the Bank of Canada has decided to increase liquidity in the financial market, and I think the result is promising. There has been a drop of nearly 1 per cent in the interest rate. That is a good way to encourage stability in the markets.

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister knows, the crisis which the world is now facing in terms of the decline in stock market values has already vastly exceeded what happened in 1929.
It is encouraging that principal industrial countries are responding in a quicker and more positive direction than was the case in 1929.
However, this having been said, does the Minister not think that it would be useful for the G-7 actually to have a meeting to try to co-ordinate on a global basis an economic strategy to head off what followed 1929?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the views of the Hon. Member. What I should say to him is that we have been having meetings of the Group of Seven on a regular basis. We had our last meeting at the end of September in Washington, at which time a number of matters were discussed.
As I indicated earlier, there have been discussions yesterday and today with members of the Group of Seven. We have compared the situations in each other's markets and compared what we can do to address the great instability or volatility in the stock markets.
However, the result of the decisions we have already taken has been good stability in the foreign exchange markets and a drop in interest rates. I think that, as a preliminary approach to the effects of the drop in the stock market, this is a good one.
We will be watching it very closely. We will be consulting on an ongoing basis. If it is appropriate to have a meeting of the G-7 countries, then we can proceed on that basis at that time.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has said that the G-7 has been meeting on a regular basis. That is true, but the last meeting was two weeks ago. To understate it a wee bit, the world has changed a little since then. The one concrete change announced by the Minister which has taken place here, which is encouraging and is in the right direction, is the move to keep interest rates down. That is the sole initiative, if I understood the Minister correctly today, which the Government of Canada plans to take.

October 20, 1987
Oral Questions
Again, does the Minister not think now is the time that the Government of Canada, in a constructive way, propose to other members of the G-7 that their Ministers of Finance get together for a meeting to map out a strategy to head off a deepening of this very serious crisis?
Mr. Speaker, we did map out a strategy at the meeting we had in the Louvre in February of this year that has served the seven countries and the world well.
The results were a little questionable.
It has not worked very well.
The Hon. Member says that it has not worked out well. Since then we have seen a remarkable degree of growth, particularly in the Canadian economy. We have good stability and exchange rates.
A trillion dollars lost in one day.
The Hon. Member said the Canadian dollar has gone down since then. That is not true, it has gone up since then.
I said a trillion dollar loss.

In that meeting we agreed as countries to undertake certain policy initiatives. The Americans have followed through on theirs as have the Japanese, the Germans, the Canadians and the other countries. We have a strategy. We have been following it and the underlying economies, as I have said, are operating very effectively. I think that is a tribute to the success of that strategy developed at the Louvre.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-DISPUTE SETTLEMENT MECHANISM
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister has just informed us he had no plans for calling a meeting of the Ministers of the Group of Seven, and that he has taken steps to provide for a temporary drop in interest rates. Does the Minister have any other measures in mind to reassure investors and to start the process of economic rebuilding that will be necessary after the past two days decline on the stock market?

Mr. Speaker, 1 think the conclusions which the Hon. Member is drawing are, to choose my words carefully, somewhat excessive. We have a strong economy. We have an economy that has performed extremely well this year, let alone over the past three years, under a strong economic plan which has been clearly followed by our Government. It has resulted in the nearly one million jobs that have been created and in Canada leading the G-7 countries in economic growth, productivity performance and job creation.
I am not denying that we have had a major drop in the stock markets. That is evident. But what I think we must not do is jump to conclusions that might not be warranted by the facts. We should watch to see what happens with the markets over the next few days and weeks and then we can have a look to see whether some further policy response is necessary. Let us not jump to conclusions.

Mr. Speaker, we face a situation in which the Toronto market has dropped by some 35 per cent from its peak for this year, in which there has been a world-wide crisis on the stock exchanges which is only outmatched by what happened back in the 1929 crash and the Great Depression of the 1930s.
Simply, apart from a temporary reduction in interest rates, does the Minister have any other specific and concrete measures in mind which he can inform the House of now, or is he still taking a wait and see attitude?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I think that all Hon. Members should be quite careful about the type of rhetoric which they use in addressing questions.
I have made it quite clear that I am in continuing touch with my colleagues in the G-7 countries so that we can review the situation on an ongoing basis. subtopic: TABLING IN GENEVA OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATING PROPOSAL ON AGRICULTURE

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: TABLING IN GENEVA OF CANADIAN NEGOTIATING PROPOSAL ON AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the Government is today tabling in Geneva a comprehensive negotiating proposal on agriculture in the Uruguay Round of the multilateral trade negotiations. It seeks to enlist the support of all GATT countries for a wide-ranging attack on trade barriers and on subsidies which distort production and trade. It is a major assault on the forces of protectionism.
Of course, we recognize that governments need to respond to the imperatives of their agricultural sectors. We are not saying that governments should not support farmers. We do say that support should be given in ways that do not distort production and trade and that are in conformity with agreed rules.
I am sure that all Hon. Members are aware of the importance which the Government attaches to agriculture. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has taken the lead to raise the issue at the past two economic summits. At Venice he secured from world leaders an acknowledgment of the need to proceed quickly in the GATT negotiations. Various Canadian Ministers have, in different international forums, advanced Canada's view that there is an urgent need for agricultural trade reform.
My colleagues and I worked hard at the OECD ministerial meeting to obtain endorsation of the general principles which should guide the reform of policies which affect agricultural trade. Over the past year I have used a series of meetings with
trade ministers from key countries to promote the development of the political will necessary to translate rhetoric into reality.
Most recently my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), spoke eloquently to the ministerial meeting of the Inter-American Institute for Co-operation in Agriculture about the need to reform agricultural trade.
I co-chaired the ministerial meeting of the Cairns Group in Ottawa this May. This is a group of 14 countries, both developed and developing, with important agricultural interests which have decided to work together to seek a major reform of the rules governing agricultural trade.
My colleagues, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State (Grains and Oil Seeds) (Mr. Mayer), and I used that meeting to build further international support for the need for the Uruguay Round of GATT negotiations to deal expeditiously and comprehensively with the problems plaguing agricultural trade. Again last week the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting adopted the Vancouver Declaration on World Trade, a Canadian initiative which re-emphasized the urgency of action on agricultural trade and agreed "on the crucial need for reform of all trade distorting agricultural policies, both domestic and international".
One imperative has clearly emerged from international discussions over the past few months, that is, that the world needs to adopt a comprehensive approach to agricultural trade reform. The OECD has demonstrated that only a broad approach covering all commodities, all countries, and all policies which directly or indirectly affect trade can have any hope of success.
The negotiations in Geneva involve 94 countries whose interests span the whole range of world agricultural production. If we are to have a successful negotiation we must deal with the legitimate concerns and interests of all countries, large and small, developed and developing, exporters and importers. We all know that many of our farmers are suffering, and suffering deeply, from the current agricultural trade crisis. We have promised not to abandon them in the short term and to seek lasting solutions in the longer term.
The proposal we are tabling today in Geneva is designed to achieve that latter goal. While our current programs are aimed at dealing with the symptoms of the problems, we will be using the Geneva negotiations to promote the basic reforms which must occur if we are to get at the underlying causes of the problem.
We are proposing that, in the longer term, over a time frame to be negotiated, all access barriers and all subsidies which distort trade should be eliminated. We consider that, in an interim period of perhaps five years starting from the conclusion of the negotiations, a major reduction should be made in all access barriers and trade-distorting subsidies.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we are firmly convinced that there is a pressing need for clear and effective GATT rules. Policymakers need to know clearly what actions they can undertake
October 20, 1987

to support their farmers. They need to know what kinds of actions will create trade problems and which ones will not. For example, the Canadian system of supply management is in conformity with GATT rules, in contrast with the open-ended support programs of some other countries which have generated massive surpluses.
The world needs to reduce the frictions which have come to characterize agricultural trade relations. Governments need to have clear rules and traders need to know that conditions of access to international markets will be secure.
The Canadian proposal is the second one to be tabled at Geneva and it should reinforce the push toward reform of the agricultural trading system. We have been working very closely with our Cairns Group partners in developing the ideas which are included in the Canadian proposal, and we are confident that the contribution by that group will also serve to promote our common objectives.
Over the rest of this year, we expect other countries will table negotiating proposals of their own. We look forward to seeing the proposals of the European Community, Japan and other major agricultural countries.
Early in the New Year negotiators in Geneva will be working to maximize the common ground in the various proposals which will have been put forward. We are seeking to reach agreement by the end of 1988 on a negotiating framework for agriculture.
These discussions will be arduous, but we are determined to make progress quickly so that Canadian farmers can begin to obtain relief from the current crisis in agricultural trade.
We are reaping today the results of 40 years of the lack of will of the GATT countries to deal effectively with agricultural problems. GATT countries recognize that we must all mend our ways. Canada is proposing a bold and far-reaching plan to achieve this goal because we know that Canadian farmers need their foreign markets to survive. Canadian farmers are among the most productive in the world. Given a level playing field, they can compete on world markets. Our negotiating proposal offers a way to do that.
We believe that a systematic attack on measures that distort trade is urgently needed. We want to create an environment where farm production decisions are more responsive to market signals. We have seen how export subsidies directly, and domestic subsidies indirectly, can distort and depress international prices. It is time that we returned some sanity to agricultural trade.
By tabling our proposal we are challenging our trading partners to join with us in the search for lasting solutions to the agricultural crisis we face today. We look forward to working with our GATT partners to define those solutions. We believe the solutions we are offering are good ones and we encourage all GATT countries to table their own ideas. In that
Statements by Ministers
way we can move directly toward an agreement which will meet the needs of the international community. In that process, all countries will need to take account of the points of view of others so that the final result of the MTN will reflect a true world view of the solutions needed.

Those programs were introduced in order to deal with our geography and certain Canadian circumstances.
Will those matters be on the table? Is that what the Minister for International Trade is talking about? Essentially she is saying that the Government will provide a few welfare handouts in the short term while it negotiates away those major subsidies. Those are legitimate questions that western Canadian farmers, in fact all farmers, will have to ask because we have seen what has happened with the proposed agricultural initiatives under the free trade proposal.
That in itself gives a number of important clues about the Government's policy. First, it abandoned the subsidy under the Western Grain Transportation Act for the movement of Canola to the United States. It is the first time that a Canadian government has ever acknowledged that a transportation subsidy is in fact a trade related subsidy. It has established a seriously dangerous precedent.
It has agreed with the Americans who challenged the WGTA and said it was a trade related subsidy. If the Government of Canada has acknowledged this to the Americans, other countries will wonder whether Canada will acknowledge it to them as well. Therefore, the whole freight rate structure upon which Canadian agriculture is very dependent will be
part of that negotiation and that so-called new reduction of subsidies about which the Government of Canada is talking.
Let me give a further example. The Government says that it will once again defend supply-management. However, if we consider the free trade agreement, we realize that when the quotas are removed and the tariff is reduced, one of the fundamental ingredients of a supply management system is pulled away.

How is it possible to organize supply management when you remove the kind of regulator by which other cheaper goods can come in and compete with your own supply system? The Government does not seem to understand most matters dealing with trade. The country was much better off when the Minister was away from the trade negotiations. The fact is that that subsidy arrangement with which we are now dealing in the tariff area is a frontal attack upon the supply-management system. That is very clearly seen in the free trade agreement and is something with which we are going to have to cope. It is not going to be part of the Canadian agricultural proposal? Is that what the Minister means? If she does not, she should spell it out much more effectively.
Let me give you another example, Mr. Speaker. We have under the free trade agreement a proposal dealing with the total reductions of the mark-ups on American wines. That does not include European wines which are the largest agricultural export commodity of the European Common Market. We are going to give the Americans lower access but we are not going to give it to the Europeans whose first response will be a challenge under the most favoured nation principle of GATT.
How can one provide a discriminatory ruling in respect of its major agricultural product and then try to get the Europeans to reduce their other kinds of barriers? The Government walks around with two right feet, continually stumbling over them. It does not know what it is doing. All it is doing is putting out a statement that is designed more to confuse and contradict than it is to give any clear explanation.
We challenge the Minister. We want to see more specifically what it is the Government is putting on the table; what kinds of tariffs, what kinds of subsidies, what kinds of programs, so that Canadian farmers will not be greeted with the same kind of fear and apprehension that met them two weeks ago when the Minister negotiated a so-called free trade agreement that will put agriculture in jeopardy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in representing my Party's response to the Minister's statement on the multilateral rounds through GATT, I would like to make a couple of observations this afternoon.
First, I want to congratulate the Minister for initiating this multilateral series of agreements and negotiations. It is a
October 20, 1987

policy decision that I wish she and her Government had adhered to in the past couple of years. Multilateral agreements make much more sense for a country the size of Canada with the kinds of trading relations we have developed over the years.
I think they will be much more productive in the long run. At least 1 certainly hope they will be much more productive than the bilateral agreements she and her colleagues came to just last week.
I note that the Minister takes some pride in the number of times the Government has raised the question of agricultural trade at the various international forums; the Cairn's Round, the Uruguay Round, the Venice Summit and the Commonwealth meeting. At all of those meetings, agriculture was mentioned.
This gives farmers some heart, but they still note that after more than two years of these kinds of meetings there is still no movement toward a basic resolution of the problem, which is basically a problem initiated by two of the largest grain traders in the world, the European Economic Community and the United States of America. The former had introduced a relatively modest, in today's terms, system of exporting grains at lower prices than they were being sold for within the European Economic Community. That in turn drew the ire of the United States, and some other competitors, of course, but the response of the United States is the one that has hurt us, and all other grain exporters, with the ultimate harm being done to exporters of meats, because it is very difficult to compete in a meat market where the extremely cheap subsidized grains are part of the input of the finishing of that meat.
The response of the U.S. was one of simply lowering what it called its loan rate, which has a habit of becoming the price for world grain. It would be very simple to change that decision made by the United States, and simply reverse it, by raising the loan rate by $1.50. Most farmers producing grains for export in the world right now would be able to come close to meeting their costs, but the U.S. refuses to do this. It chooses instead to use its treasury to pay its farmers instead of demanding that price from the market. The multilateral approach under GATT, while I must say I admire it, has some very large shortcomings in this particular set of initiatives which I think all farmers recognize, particularly if they are exporters of grains.
The GATT round includes 94 countries but does not include as full participants the U.S.S.R. or the People's Republic of China, the two largest grains importers in the world. As well they are two of the largest producers of grain in the world.

speechtext:
Yes, China and Russia are the two largest producers. While China has observer status, as I interpret it, from outside, it appears the U.S.A. is trying to keep the U.S.S.R. from participating in these talks. I am quite concerned about that because it brings back memories from ten or 15 years ago of the United States trying to set the rules for the
Statements by Ministers
international grain talks that were going on at that time. The Americans had a firm idea in their heads about who should be considered producers and who should be considered consumers.
In the American view, Japan and the European Economic Community should be on the consumer side forever and ever, amen; the United States and other select groups of countries would be considered to be producers, and there would be certain rules and regulations for the two sides to take part, and that would be how the world markets would be carved up forever after. Unfortunately, the U.S. assessment was wrong. I think its assessment of keeping the U.S.S.R. out of these discussions is equally wrong. It was only a short period of time before both Japan and the EEC became exporters or had export capabilities in the production of grain. There has to be in these rounds recognition that countries do have the capability to switch from being consumers to being producers and exporters of grains.
I hold that both China and Russia have excellent opportunities to become surplus producers, given a climate where subsidies in the more developed countries disappear. I remind the House, because I think a lot of Members are not aware of this, that the U.S.S.R produces grain on a cost-of-production basis. Its state farms have to price the grain out at their actual costs. That is not the case for the production in Canada or in the United States. We sell the grain for what it will bring and it is usually below actual production costs.
As long as the Russians are functioning that way, they are very rational economic beings. They purchase grain because it is cheaper for them to purchase it than it is for them to produce it. But as soon as we and the other so-called more developed countries drop our subsidization program and stop using our tax dollars to subsidize the export of grains, those countries will become competitive and they have the capability to increase production. As soon as prices go up they will indeed increase production. So any agreement, whether under the GATT or as a special grains agreement, that ignores the Soviet Union is doomed to failure.
I think the program announced today does not provide us with very many details. I thank the Minister, however, for having made the effort. I think we are still awaiting an announcement and the tabling of documents from the Department of Agriculture, which has been doing an in depth analysis of what programs are now being provided in this country which would not meet the criteria that Canada has put forward at international meetings. These programs should be tabled for our review. It is not clear from this statement whether the Special Grains Program of last year will be permitted to continue this year. Farmers want to know, as quickly as possible, whether that $2.6 billion to $3 billion will be made available to them this year. Their very lives depend on it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the House rose at one o'clock there were two minutes left in the question and comment period of the speech of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). Are there any questions or comments?
Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak on this Bill because it has serious implications for the future of our country. Certainly, over the years the whole immigration process and refugee designation has become so cumbersome that we have had no idea what we were actually doing as far as immigration was concerned.
I know that this Bill was put forward in an attempt to straighten out some of those issues, but instead it only adds to the inequality and the injustices that have already stayed in the system. When we look at some of the main thoughts of Bill C-55, we must look at the fact that there is a denial of rights to be heard. That is in direct contravention of the Accord that we have signed, which in Article 33 states that "no country shall expel or return a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where their life or freedom would be threatened on account of their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular group, or social opinion". This means that when we do not allow a refugee to be heard, we are in direct contravention of the treaty that we signed.
In 1976, the Immigration Act was such that often officials were illegally turning people back without having heard them. When a stop was put to that, instead of this system becoming streamlined and efficient, there was a horrendous backlog. In an attempt to rid ourselves of this backlog, we have in front of the House Bill C-55.
Unfortunately, Bill C-55 does not get rid of the backlog. It gets rid of genuine refugees. That is the great concern that I have. Not only do people not have a right to be heard, but they have no time to prepare themselves for the hearing. There is no
higher authority of appeal that has always been there. When we asked for an amendment in order that at least the chairman of the review committee could act in the next stage of appeal, that was refused. It seems to me that what we are looking at is something that traditionally is not what we would want as a society.
Unfortunately, there are many Canadians who do not believe that this type of thing is happening. They think that we are opening up and streamlining our system. It is important that we take a good look at this Bill and recognize that we are saying, "Sorry, if your life is in danger, if you are fleeing, you cannot come to Canada unless you have a visa, unless you have gone to your travel agent and acquired a ticket and you arrive here as a tourist". Basically, that is what we are saying.
When we recognize no safe third country, and look at what is a safe third country, very often we will not allow people to be admitted to Canada from another country. We have no assurances that those countries will keep them for a hearing. We are only saying that we will not hear them. We are really saying that we do not value their lives, therefore, it is all right for them to go back where they can continue to be persecuted and very often executed.
That is a tragedy and a mark on the very forward-looking attempt by the former Prime Minister, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), when he raised the quotas of the Southeast Asian refugees and had them coming into this country. When looking back at that experience of almost 10 years, we will recognize that those people contributed to the economy of this country, to its character, to its culture, and certainly to its future.
It does not take very long for us to do a quick summary of some of the people who came at that time. They went through dire circumstances. They did not have legitimate papers. They did not necessarily come from safe third countries, some of which we would designate today as safe third countries. We opened our gates and welcomed them. They were privately sponsored and they have done very well. They have given Canada a whole sense and thread of culture that previously we did not have in the fabric of our country. I think it has been very important.
That will not happen again. What will happen if this Bill goes through is, unfortunately, something that has been on the agenda of the bureaucrats of the Department for many years. They will be the ones who will decide offshore who is and who is not a refugee. They will decide who is the best economic type of person to let into our country. Through their bureaucratic policies, they will decide what is or what is not humane. That is not the manner in which we have made decisions in the past.
Because there has been a backlog in our refugee designation, all we have done is to bend to what they have been attempting to do for approximately 20 years. Now they are successful. They are the ones who will decide the future of this country, as far as immigration is concerned. In looking not only at
October 20, 1987

refugees but at regular immigrants who wish to bring in or sponsor a relative, if there has been some official decision made, the whole process of appeal is so cumbersome and lengthy that they will never get into the country. Those are the people who are now complaining that they have been waiting. They will not cost the country any money because they are willing to sponsor their relatives and willing to sign the commitment for the people coming in. Certainly, because there has been an infrastructure of family and relatives there, they will be the solid type of people whom we wish to have in our country in the future. We are eliminating a lot of this.
We are putting issues to a very arbitrary type of decisionmaking when we say that, if a refugee is heard, he has to be heard very quickly, with no time for preparation. They are very fearful of what their conditions are, very often they are not knowledgeable in either of our official languages and, therefore, they have no way of being able to be heard legitimately, whether or not their lives are in danger or they are being persecuted.
We must also keep in mind the fact that we are only taking in approximately 5 per cent of the world refugees in the western world. When we are taking such a small number of refugees in the western world, it seems a tragedy that we are being selective and arbitrary about our decisions. What we are saying is that we do not really care whether or not people's lives are in danger. What we really want is to look at people who are in trouble and say to them that it is not their lives that we are worried about, it is what type of skills they have and what occupation they will have in our country. In that case, we may let them in, but then again we may not. If they are already here, they will be heard quickly. We will never be able to hear them out thoroughly and, therefore, very often their attempt at designation as refugee will not be heard.
Not only is this unfair and unjust, but it is very un-Canadian. It is not the type of thing that our country has responded to in the past. If we look at the refugees that we have opened our doors to, it has always been a positive experience. At times we have become arbitrary and turned it over to the officials of the Department, which unfortunately was what the decisionmaking was in 1939.
If we read None Was Too Many, which was documentation of the whole process of immigration at that time, we find that bureaucrats in the Department placed an over-emphasis on their decision-making power. With that kind of power they arbitrarily turned people away from our shores. They were sent back to the gas chambers, and we said that it was okay. That has been a blot on our history.
However, we can look back to the wonderful experience of opening our doors to the Hungarians, to the southeast Asians, and to many other refugees. Each time we did that, Canada had a spurt of growth and certainly its mosaic was enriched. We also had a good feeling about ourselves because were were
Immigration Act, 1976
putting our hands out to our brothers and sisters around the world. We were saying that we were not a country which only makes bureaucratic decisions but we are a country which is capable of looking at the whole.
When we signed the international agreement we were complimented by the United Nations. At that time we were told that Canada was in the lead and that Canada was showing generosity. What have we done since? We have contravened the agreement so that the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees has criticized us.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not true, Mr. Speaker.
I am sorry, but I have certainly received some correspondence to that effect.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, your correspondence is false. That is not true.

Mr. Speaker, I think I will respond to the questions after, but that is the kind of correspondence I have received.
Over the years we have worked hard to ensure that our reputation would be sustained. I think the Hon. Member who is saying that that is not true took a very personal and active part in ensuring that we would have that kind of generous policy. It grieves and upsets me to say that everyone has been caught in this and that they have succumbed to bureaucratic decisions.
We have talked about the kind of Canada we want when discussing a variety of other Bills. However, surely the whole essence of that is how we treat people individually. If we do not start looking at people as part of the human family, we do not understand the human family or what our planet is all about. It seems to me that this Bill contravenes the goals and visions of our country over the years.
We will be told by our children and our grandchildren that it was because of this kind of Bill that people lost their lives. That is not the reputation we want to build for ourselves. That is not the reputation we want for this country. We have lots of land. We have lots of resources. We have the ability to be humane.
Even though our immigration numbers have been high, we have not met the quotas year after year. We have often been short. We have been short for the last two years or three years. We will probably continue to be short. If we pass a Bill like this one, we certainly will not be able to meet the quotas of people who are trying to save their lives, people who are escaping.
It is important to look at the demography of the country in very practical terms, at what is happening to our birth rate, and at the recognition that we need to increase immigration to maintain our population. We need that population if we are to develop a buoyant and vibrant economy. However, if we continue to bring in restrictive Bills such as this one, we might

October 20, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
not even be getting the kind of people we want, because Canada will soon be known to be a country which does not look generously and humanely at people, but as a country which looks at its own economic objectives with no sense of what are the rights of persons to survival.
1 am very concerned that we are continuing to consider this Bill and that some of the amendments we have put forward were not accepted. 1 think they were very slight amendments. We were hoping that they would soften the Bill so that maybe a few lives would be saved which will not now be saved. We recognize that there are people who probably are not qualified to make decisions on whether or not a refugee is a refugee, who are not qualified for refugee designation. However, over and above that is the fact that the hearing and the information will be so short and incomplete that even if they were qualified it would be very difficult for them to make a good decision.
We know some of the things that are happening in Central America now. We know that the United States has closed its doors on refugees. I remind the House that we are only talking about 5 per cent of refugees who are coming into the western world. We realize that maybe the lives of people coming to Canada from Central America can be saved.
According to the Bill, if they do not have their papers, their visas, or their travel agent tickets, we will say "no" and send them back to the United States. The United States has said that it will not keep them, so they will be sent back to where they have been tortured and persecuted. That is not the kind of Bill at which we should be looking or of which we should be proud. We should be ashamed of this Bill, and we should not want to see it expedited.
We recognize the backlog in terms of refugee designation. Clearly something needed to be done. When they attempted to straighten that out, what happened was that the refugee designation system became backlogged because they allowed bureaucrats to make decisions and they did not put in place a decision which streamlined the system and provided adequate time, resources, and staff to ensure that they were heard.
It is no secret that for many years the Department has said that it knew better than anyone else who should come to Canada. With this Bill they are saying that the only people who will be able to designate refugees are our officials who decide what camps to go to, to pick out the cream of the crop, and to send them here. That is a dreadful direction for us to take both in immigration and in refugee designation. It seems to me that there is a better way to do things. We could streamline. We could have two parallel systems, one that is identifying and designating refugees and another which is looking at straight immigration. We also need to increase the family reunification program and our resources for refugee designation.
It is not an impossible task, but what they are doing is just taking 10 backward steps in attempting to amend the Immigration Act with this Bill. I urge Hon. Members of the House to defeat the Bill because it is not the kind of thing of which
any of us will ever be proud. It is the kind of thing that can leave us with a legacy where people will say: "What were they thinking of? Did they have no sense of justice and humanity? When the world was getting into a turmoil, what did Canada do?" They will say that Canada restricted its immigration Bill so badly that it was literally impossible for refugees to have their lives saved by coming to this country.

Mr. Speaker, 1 congratulate the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) on a speech which I think was a very powerfully reasoned and moral plea. I think the moral issue she presented is right and was very strongly stated.
Although it is only a few months since she was elected in Hamilton Mountain, I know that she spent a good deal of time talking with the people there before she was elected and that she has been in close touch with them since she was elected. I would like to ask her what she finds about the opinion of the people of Hamilton Mountain or anywhere else that she wishes to mention.
My point is that we were told by the Government that Canadian people all want this harsh law. We have been told that groups like the churches, refugee aid groups, and the Bar Association representing 35,000 lawyers who opposed the Bill were only special interest or pressure groups speaking against the majority of the public.
I would be interested to know what the Hon. Member has found about the expression of opinion from the public in her particular area of jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I have been to meetings in my riding of Hamilton Mountain. I have had correspondence from groups right across the country. 1 have had calls from individuals in Hamilton Mountain. The general thrust is that people want to have a fair Immigration Act. They have heard the debate and looked at the Bill and recognized that this is not a fair Bill. It is a Bill that will discriminate against refugee designation. Certainly the consensus that I have heard in my riding from the people of Hamilton Mountain, from some of the collective groups, the church groups, the local labour council, individual parishes and congregations is that we should speak out against the Bill. They would like to stop it because they think it is a backward step and one which will give us an international reputation of not being the just and generous society which they like to think we are.
I think it would be less than responsible if we did not speak out against the Bill. The information I get from the people who have elected me to represent them is that Canada needs a fair and just immigration Bill. This we do not have. Some people have been generously wanting to sponsor family members, but they have been unable to do that. They have wanted to sponsor refugees, but have been stopped from doing that. With the other Bill coming through, people could be charged for helping
October 20, 1987

refugees and could be seen as being criminals in what they thought was an act of charity and love.
1 have no hesitation in being able to say to the Hon. Member that the people of my riding and in the district in which my riding is, Hamilton Wentworth, have organized meetings, as have the churches. They have made a plea to us to speak out against the Bill. I spent about an hour in my office just before we came into the House today responding to correspondence asking me to to please do something about this Bill which they are against. It seems to me that we are representing the people who elected us to speak for them as well as for the potential future immigrants who will not now be able to come to this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned church groups in her riding. Were they of one particular religious orientation or do they include non-Christian groups? Did they indicate a knowledge of what is in the Bill so that the Member felt they knew what they were opposing, or were they only speaking generally for fairness?

Mr. Speaker, the churches, including synagogues and Muslim groups as well as Christian groups, have studied the Bill. They have looked at the lack of a safe third country provision as well as a lack of a provision for a just and adequate hearing. They recognize that there is no avenue for a higher appeal. The know the Bill very well. They fear that there is a sort of popular approach to the introduction of the Bill. People thought that it would be harmless and it would not be as obstructive as it actually is. I think church congregations have been very successful in getting that concern out. We are hearing from the individual citizens now as well as from the collective groups. It seems to me that not only have they studied the Bill but they are doing a good job at educating people around them about what the Bill is all about. I have come across people who at first said they supported the Bill but when they got the Bill and started to look into it they came out in great opposition. The more and more people know about the Bill the more concerned they are about it.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned the matter of no safe third country. We know that particular phrase has been removed from the Bill.
Will the Hon. Member comment on the fact that the United Nations representative came to the committee to speak about the Bill and agreed with one of the government questioners that the UN does not charge Canada with contravening the Convention? But it was pointed out by a later witness that, of course, the UN does not charge us with contravention because there is no such thing as enforcement. There is no policeman to take us into court or put us in jail over this Convention.
Immigration Act, 1976
We have all seen the four page letter which was sent, which matter was reiterated in greater detail before the committee. There was a demand that there be a guarantee against refoulement of anyone who might be a refugee. One of the questions raised is whether the principle that a person be sent back to a country considered to be in compliance with Article 33 of the Convention is satisfied given the fact that it does not guarantee that such a country will give a person a hearing which Canada denied.
Does the Hon. Member consider that, by failing to ensure that either Canada or the country of departure give a refugee claimant a hearing, we have in fact refused to meet the request of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees on that point? Second, when people had studied the Bill they asked for an adequate appeal system. As Members know, no change was made in that respect. Would the Hon. Member consider on that point that we fail to meet the requests? I ask these questions because the Hon. Member got some very high priced heckling from across the aisle from a Member who said that the correspondence was false. I think the heckling from across the street was false. I would like the Hon. Member to make her comment.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question in my mind, even though we took out the no safe third country concept, that if Canada does not give an adequate hearing, and we have no guarantee that an adequate hearing will be had from the country to which the person is returned, we are contravening the agreement. Some of the rationale I have heard in the debate in the House of Commons is that it is not our fault that the other country will not give people a hearing. We have already established that precedent by saying that we as a country will not do it, so why should we expect somebody else to do it. I certainly do not think that we met the request from the United Nations High Commissioner. What was being asked was to make sure that we did not contravene the convention in that way.
As well, the appeal process I have described is not there. We even asked for something as minor as to have the chairman of the refugee commission review the process, but that was refused. It seems that we literally do not have an appeal process per se, certainly not the type of appeal process asked for by the High Commissioner. There is no question in my mind that we can be held up for criticism in that we did not meet the conditions. After having signed the agreement we have obviously said we really do not care about it, that if somebody else does not care about it, that is their problem. We are not doing anything to show any leadership about any kind of moral commitment to the resolution of a world problem on which the western world is not going overboard, but for the little bit we do take responsibility we are not taking a lot of moral responsibility. I do think it is a shame.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter the debate. The constituency I represent has for 100 years been the place in which new immigrants and refugees who came to western Canada first settled. To the people who came from eastern Europe before World War I, the Ukrainians, the Poles, the Germans, the Jews and the Czechs, to mention just a few of the groups, in recent years have been added people from Italy, Portugal, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Viet Nam, Central America, Africa-it would take all my time to list all of the countries from which people have come.
The record of Canada with respect to the entry of immigrants and refugees prior to and during World War II is one of which none of us can be proud. Any Member of Parliament who has read that very important book, None is Too Many, written by Irving Abella, will know how impossible it was for Jewish refugees to enter Canada after the seizing of power in Germany by Hitler and how not only the Prime Minister of the day but indeed the senior officials of the Immigration Department worked so hard to keep out those and other refugees.
Things changed after World War II. We have seen the movement into Canada of several million people, either as immigrants or as refugees. After the end of World War II, we saw tens of thousands of people, people who had lived in the
countries of eastern Europe and who had been uprooted and pushed into western Europe as slave labourers during World War II who did not want to go back to those countries which are now communist dominated, come to Canada. Later, at the time of the revolt in Hungary, we saw thousands of Hungarians come to Canada. After the difficulties in Poland, thousands of people came from Poland. Then came Asians from Uganda, Chileans and Vietnamese. Tens of Thousands of people have come here as a result of political uprisings, unrest and revolutions and have adjusted to Canada and made important and useful contributions to Canada.

1 intend to vote against this Bill, as I have indicated right from the beginning. As I have indicated right from the beginning, 1 think this is one of the worst Bills with which Parliament has had to deal in many years. It is unfair to refugees. It will be used against many people who, I believe, have the right to come to this country. It will be used to keep out many people who, if permitted to come to this country, would make a contribution as have the hundreds of thousands of people who have come to this country since the end of World War II, either as immigrants or refugees.
I see a tremendous change in the population of my city. There are people of all races, all colours, and all religions there. People like the former Justice Clyne of British Columbia have criticized and attacked what has happened since World War II. They believe that this will destroy the country. I believe, however, that permitting people to come to this country, either as immigrants or refugees, from every continent in the world since World War II has added a great deal to our country, it has helped to make this country a much better place in which to live than it ever was before. Because I believe that this Bill will lessen the number of people whom we permit to come to this country, either as immigrants or refugees, I intend to oppose it.

Mr. Speaker, I have a number of comments to make. The rhetoric I have been listening to in this debate is starting to get to me. We seem to have overlooked the facts and it may be interesting to go back and look at some of them.
I have heard no mention of the major problem involved with the recent landing on the foggy shores of Nova Scotia of a large group of illegal aliens. That is what they should be called. The terms "refugees", "boat people" or whatever are only euphemisms for people who have deliberately broken the laws of Canada and landed on our shores without any right whatsoever. There are thousands of people throughout the world who are waiting for visas in order to come to Canada legitimately and honestly. Illegal aliens attempt to jump the queue.
When the current Immigration Act was drafted in 1976 anyone in Canada, whether here legally or illegally, was given the right to a determination of their claim by the Minister and to a redetermination before the Immigration Appeal Board of any claim rejected by the Minister. Quite frankly, that was not a bad system.
These were not simply assurances or administrative arrangements, but were rights established in the law which made it impossible to remove anyone until these rights were honoured. The current system began to break down in the early 1980s due to an unprecedented number of refugee claims which, at one point, numbered over 1,000 a week. That was caused by worldwide events beyond Canada's control. Many of
October 20, 1987

these people were claiming refugee status when in fact they were economic migrants.
That is an abuse of Canada's generosity because it constitutes an attempt to remain illegally in Canada. Some of the bona fide refugees, as well, are people from refugee-producing countries who had an opportunity to find a safe haven in another developed country before they came to Canada. Unfortunately, nothing can be done to keep such people out of our very complex process until the Immigration Act is changed.
This Bill provides us with the tools to deal with the high volumes of claimants we are experiencing. It introduces three features which are not found in the current legislation. The Member has totally ignored those three features.
First, individuals arriving from countries that have been designated as safe third countries by the Cabinet will be returned to those countries without being allowed to claim refugee status in Canada. Second, manifestly unfounded claims are refugee claims without any merit because they are based on difficulties not at all related to the Geneva Convention. Third, there will be a streamlined determination process. For persons whose claims appear to have some substance there will be a single level of review by an independent quasi-judicial tribunal and an appeal by leave to the Federal Court of Canada. This will be completed in a few months rather than in several years as is now the case.
The new refugee determination system will offer a simple, high-quality procedure moving us clearly away from the existing cumbersome system of review and appeal. It will provide effective defence against abuse and, thereby, prevent manipulation.
Does this mean that I am against refugees any more than is the Hon. Member? Of course not. I believe that legitimate individuals who, for political rather than criminal reasons, could face death if returned to their country of origin should be allowed to stay in Canada provided that they are prepared to be good citizens of Canada and to work for this country. This is a moral and responsible attitude espoused by the NDP with which I totally agree. If there is real danger to individuals, of course they should be allowed to stay.
Nine out of ten refugees are economic refugees seeking a better life in Canada. Who can blame them? However, entry to Canada must be legal and achieved in an organized and proper manner. Illegal aliens make a mockery of Canada. That is why this legislation is necessary and should be passed.
The 1976 Liberal Government Immigration Act was a humanitarian and charitable attempt to open Canada to help the rest of the world. Unfortunately, it has been used and abused by the desperate and has been overwhelmed. In the interests of all Canadians it must be changed substantially. Why the NDP does not understand that, I do not understand. In any event, let us get on with passing this Bill and cleaning up immigration in Canada.
