I heard what I said, Mr. Speaker. I do not know if you did. 1 believe it is absolutely true that part of the confusion that has arisen about this issue is the difference between immigrants and refugees, particularly in reference to those unfortunate people who landed on the shores of Nova Scotia in the summer.
No one would pretend to even argue that they were immigrants in the ordinary sense, nor would they probably be covered by this legislation. In fact, as 1 understand it, Bill C-84 itself was directed toward those people who landed on the shores of Nova Scotia during the summer months.
I suggest that the Member's comments only add to the confusion that exits in the country and perhaps to the misconception that those individuals somehow or other had denied legitimate immigration claimants access to Canada because they were queue-jumpers over legitimate immigrants. I do not think that is a fair way to characterize this problem.
I want to comment on the excellent work of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), as well as on the time he spent on this Bill both in the House and in the committee. It was a great help to members of my caucus, and I know that while government Members may disagree with him, I am sure they appreciated his contribution.
I have seldom seen any piece of legislation that has been so roundly condemned and opposed by groups and individuals who have been concerned with refugee and immigration matters over the years.
I understand that there were some 40 witnesses who appeared before the committee dealing with this Bill during some forty-four and a half hours of testimony before the committee. All of those 40 committees were in opposition to what the Government was proposing. I am told that there were probably five witnesses before the committee who supported what the Government was proposing, but most of them were officials from the Minister's Department and one was a representative of the airlines, which I believe have their own vested interest in the outcome of this Bill.
I want to read a letter concerning Bill C-55 that was circulated to concerned MP's by a Mr. Donald Anderson, General Secretary of the Canadian Council of Churches. 1 want to read it because he says what I would like to say much better. He begins:
We appreciate government work to try to improve Bill C-55. Unfortunately our deep concerns remain. How can we know if a person claiming to be a refugee needs our help if we do not hear their problems? Each person claiming to be a refugee should have a right to have their individual circumstances assessed and their case decided on its merits before competent independent decision-makers. To us, this is the intent of the Convention and Protocol.
He is talking about the United Nations Convention and Protocol to which Canada is a signatory. He goes on to say:
Immigration programs may legitimately choose who comes on humanitarian grounds and may set priorities on countries they may come from. We understand the attractiveness of this approach. Bill C-55 provides for exclusion of people not on the basis of their individual circumstances, but by a political cabinet decision that the country they transited before arriving in Canada is deemed to adhere to Clause 33 of the Convention, that is, it is deemed the transit country will not return the person in any manner whatsoever to a country where he or she may face persecution. This is a far shot from our obligation to give an individual who arrives in Canada a fair hearing of his or her claim to need our protection.
Also, there is no meaningful appeal to any of the critical decisions made which can remove claimants from Canada in proposed inquiries and hearings.
He concludes by saying:
We cannot accept legislation which sets aside a claimant's right to just procedures in the name of administrative convenience. We urge you to reconsider, to abandon this Bill C-55 and to speedily replace it with one conforming with the principles of allowing every claimant a hearing on the merits and a meaningful appeal. There are alternative processes we can surely all support.
Most of the witnesses who appear before that committee, while recognizing that there was something wrong with Canada's immigration processes, also made suggestions on how Bill C-55 could become a more humane Bill, give more consideration to the needs of those individuals who wish to establish refugee status in Canada. Unfortunately, the majority on the committee rejected all of those suggestions that were put forward.
For example, World Relief Canada, which serves as the refugee resettlement arm of the Evangelical Fellowship of Canada, an association of 23 evangelical protestant denominations, strongly urged the Government not to pass Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 as they were originally proposed. Mr. Lome Waldman of the Coalition for a Just Refugee and Immigration Policy said:
We would like to ask you to remember in your deliberations the wider context of the refugee issue.
We feel that Canada should play a role in pressing for peaceful solutions to conflicts in areas of the world that produce refugees.
In conclusion, I would simply say that I think it is unfortunate that the Government has resorted to extreme measures in reacting to what everyone admits is a problem, but which is not as big a problem as the Government is attempting to make it out to be. It is obvious that it is going to have the support of the majority of the House because it has the bodies, but I would honestly hope that at some point down the road the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) will review this policy and come up with something that is much more humane so that Canada can continue to enjoy the reputation we have managed to build up internationally with regard to our approach to refugees and to our immigration policy.

Mr. Speaker, I was not going to give a speech, but I have been moved by what I heard. I thought I would just say a few words that I want to put on the record.
October 20, 1987

Here we are in the third week of October. This House was brought back on August 10. Why was the House brought back? Do you remember why we were brought back, Mr. Speaker? First, we were brought back because in fact we were being invaded. There was a sort of Asian phobia because the Sikhs had landed on the East Coast. I recall that atmosphere very well. The Government was finally going to show how decisive and tough it was. We heard comments like "queue-jumpers". This boatload of refugees who landed on our shores and claimed refugee status were queue jumpers. They were abusing the system and it was not fair. There was a big argument and the Government mixed up refugees and immigrants until the public could not make out the difference between refugees and immigrants. The Government brought us all back on August 10 and it brought in Bill C-84 which was concocted in the crypts of the bureaucrats here in Ottawa.
The Government got the sensitive Minister-and he understands what 1 mean when I say he is a sensitive Minister and should be a sensitive Minister-to bring in Bill C-84. And where is Bill C-84 now? It has not been passed as law and Canada has not been invaded. Canada still exists and Bill C-84 is hung up. But the Government decided that while we were here it was going to jam Bill C-55 through, and here it is. We are in third reading of Bill C-55 today. The Government also thought that while we were here it was going to get Bill C-22 passed, and we all know where Bill C-22 is today. It is keeping Bill C-84 company. They are warming each other up in the warm place with the red carpet and the majority of Liberals over there, God bless their souls.
I have to ask myself what kind of government it is that cannot even order its priorities and get its legislation through. What kind of leadership is it exhibiting? It is a government that, for example, could not bear to have the Chairman, its Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, depart from the Party line, having said it believes in the independence of committees? That man showed bravery in standing up in this House and condemning Bill C-84, as well as condemning Bill C-85. He did it publicly.

I have a short question for the Hon. Member, because he can probably hit the nail on the head more quickly than many Members in the House. My question is in regard to the politics of Bill C-84 and Bill C-55.
I wish to relay what has happened in my own constituency during the last two weeks, and the type of inaction 1 have found from the government side. Last week I hand-delivered a letter to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) regarding large numbers of illegal aliens coming into my constituency by boat up the Stikine River. 1 contacted Customs in Prince Rupert. Those people had not been clearing Customs. Their state of origin was unknown. I contacted the RCMP and they told me that they did not have the budget to go up and do anything about it, but perhaps I could help by getting in touch with the Solicitor General to get something done.
I assume that the Solicitor General has been in touch with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) about it, because it is a serious matter. Those people are
entering Canada illegally. They are contravening all types of provincial and federal statutes with their activities while they are in British Columbia.
Having related that to my friend, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I would like to ask him what he thinks the politics are. Here we have an example right now of where we cannot get an immigration officer, a police officer, or anyone to deal with illegal aliens coming into northwestern British Columbia. But in a situation where a boat load of refugees arrive in Nova Scotia, suddenly it is a national crisis. Parliament has to be recalled. The House of Commons, which costs $180 million a year, has to be thrown into full force. Three months later we are still debating the Bill. Not a single one of those who came in under refugee status to Nova Scotia has been deported, asked to leave, or kept in custody.
I ask the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, what are the politics and the political agenda of the Government in recalling the House during the summer to deal with Bill C-84, and now Bill C-55?

It seemed to me that the Minister responsible for immigration should have been on his feet right away asking the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) the question as to where those people are coming from, the ones whom the Hon. Member reported to the authorities as being illegal aliens. I notice the Minister is not interested in that type of information.
The Hon. Member for Skeena asked me about the politics. Look, I am just a lowly back-bencher in the New Democratic caucus. I only look at things and size them up. I asked myself the question, "What are the politics of this situation?" Well, as I described, the Government is on the ropes, down at 23 per cent in the polls.
Twenty-eight per cent.

It is looking for something to bring it up in the polls. To its salvation comes a boat-load of Sikhs on the East Coast of Canada. Right away it is a crisis.
I saw the television cameras showing the House of Commons; the midnight oil was burning in the Minister's office; they were planning. The Armed Forces were called out. Our Navy-all two boats-was out there patrolling the 200-mile limit. Information was leaked that there was another boat on the way with the wives and the spouses. The gunboats were out, they were armed, and there they were patrolling and patrolling. This image was on the TV screens. As the image was on, the hysteria was building. It reminded me of what I had been reading in history about the hysteria that Mackenzie King used to whip up against the CCF and the yellow race.
Of course, here was the Government determined to pull itself up by the boot straps from 23 per cent, and here was this golden opportunity to show how tough it was. That is the politics behind that.
October 20, 1987

Furthermore, it is no secret that the Government knew that a lot of that animosity towards the Sikhs had been whipped up in this country. Even if there were some violent ones, it was applied to the whole community of Sikhs, which is very unfortunate and very untrue. So here was the situation of this boat-load. It had an appropriate group, the Government was going to come in with Bill C-84 and recall Parliament. We all know that Parliament can only be recalled if it is an emergency situation. The Speaker had to be convinced that this was an emergency situation, and Your Elonour was convinced of it and acquiesced to recalling Parliament.
I imagine that the stock market could have been falling and we would never have been called back. But this was a national crisis. We had to solve this problem of 200 people. Well, 1 think that is the politics of it. It is really a disreputable situation.
The Government will inherit the disaster that will follow from this type of action. It has not improved its standing in the polls. It will find out, as have all Governments in the past, that playing this type of game will catch up with it in the end.

that Bill C-214, an Act to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am honoured and pleased, under the new rules of the House, to have before us Bill C-214, an Act to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone.
The main contents of the Bill are the declaration of Canada, our territorial seas and airspace, as nuclear weapons free. It also calls for Canada, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), at the earliest opportunity to move a motion calling for a world referendum on world disarmament.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the former Hon. Member for The Battlefords

Meadow Lake, have had similar Bills before the House for debate. The Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), who is present for the debate this evening, has a votable motion presently before the House to declare Canada a nuclear arms free zone, to prohibit export of materials or technology for construction or deployment of nuclear arms, and to encourage cities, provinces, and states throughout the world to undertake similar action.
Many recent publications have come out, but one of the better ones, in my view, is the one by Elizabeth Woodworth, a medical historian in Victoria in my home province of British Columbia. She has put together a book called What can I do? Citizen's Strategies for Nuclear Disarmament. In one of its appendices there are a number of quotations from military professionals and statesmen about war and nuclear weapons with which 1 should like to lead in the debate.
I should like to quote first from Admiral Noel Gayler, U.S. Navy (Retired) Former Director of the National Security Agency, Commander of all U.S. Forces in the Pacific, and Deputy Director of the Joint Strategic Target Planning Staff. He had the following to say:

October 20, 1987
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
There is no sensible military use for any of our nuclear forces: intercontinental, theater, or tactical.
The second quote is from McGeorge Bundy, George F. Kennan, Roberts S. McNamara, and Gerard Smith, from the paper they produced called Nuclear Weapons and the Atlantic Alliance, and I quote:
It is time to realize that no one has ever succeeded in advancing any persuasive reason to believe that any use of nuclear weapons, even on the smallest scale, could reliably be expected to remain limited.
The third quote is from Chairman Leonid Brezhnev at the 26th Communist Party Congress in Moscow. He said the following:
The peoples should know the truth about the consequences, ruinous for mankind, which nuclear war would bring.
The next quote is from President Ronald Reagan in his recent Camp David address, and I quote:
A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
The next quotation is from Rear Admiral Eugene J. Carroll, U.S. Navy (Retired) and currently Deputy Director of the Centre for Defence Information in Washington, D.C., in Nuclear War: The Search for Solutions, from the proceedings of a conference held at the University of British Columbia under the auspices of Physicians for Social Responsibility just a year ago, and I quote:
You simply can't fight with nuclear weapons, and the first lesson that we have learned as we build up these arsenals is that they serve no rational military purpose.
"-Both sides are planning, arming, and training for a nuclear war. We are on a collision course in the name of deterrence. Each side says we are building these weapons to deter nuclear war, we are preparing for a war to have peace. We are going to end up with the weapons themselves starting a war which no one wants. They are going to be uncontrollable and unmanageable in time of crisis or under events of stress, miscalculation, or accident.
1 want to comment on that quotation for a moment. Just yesterday and today we learned the impact of having massive amounts of so-called co-ordinated hardware and software in terms of the computers involved in the New York Stock Exchange, Toronto Stock Exchange, Vancouver, Hong Kong, London, and around the world.
We realize that if there is anything we can learn from that, it is not just that the stock market is a barometer but that one of the fixes which has come to be involved in that area of the world market-place is the same kind of technology which is involved throughout the world in terms of a nuclear response in a time of crisis. I think we can just hope that the same kind of thought processes which put the chips together for computers monitoring the equity market are not the same kind of thought processors that put together the response mechanisms for the computer hardware for a nuclear response.
The next quote I have is from Dwight D. Eisenhower, 34th President of the United States, who said:
When people speak to you about a preventive war, you tell them to go and fight it. After my experience, I have come to hate war. War settles nothing.
The next quote is from Dr. George F. Kennan, U.S. Ambassador to the Soviet Union in his speech of acceptance of the Albert Einstein Peace Prize in 1981 who said:
To my mind, the nuclear bomb is the most useless weapon ever invented. It can be employed to no rational purpose. It is not even an effective defence against itself... I question whether these devices are really weapons at all.
The next quote is from Churchill, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940-1945 and 1951-1955. He said:
The human tragedy reaches its climax in the fact that after all the exertions and sacrifices of hundreds of millions of people and the victories of the Righteous Cause we have still not found Peace or Security and that we lie in the grip of even worse perils than those we have surmounted.
The last quote is from Albert Einstein. In the final week of his life, in his last signed appeal against the development of nuclear weapons, he said:
We appeal, as human beings, to human beings: Remember your humanity, and forget the rest.
Many learned and thoughtful people have set their minds on how to deal realistically with the nuclear presence we now find on the planet. There are over 50,000 nuclear weapons, all of them larger than those which eliminated, in the blink of an eye, Nagasaki and Hiroshima. We have to become much more practical. That is why I am encouraged to see so many publications coming out, so many Canadians, physicians and people around the world regardless of nationality, rallying to a common cause to find a way to denuclearize the world through verifiable and balanced means so that the world can go on quite a different course.
There are nuclear weapons free zones by international treaties, the four key ones being the sea bed, Antarctica, outer space and Central America. Seventeen nations around the world have already self-declared, including Japan, Austria, Sweden and New Zealand most recently. Work is under way to declare the South Pacific nuclear free, and hopefully through efforts in this House, if we can manage to get enough Members mobilized on it, to get first a Canadian declaration and ultimately an international treaty to declare Canada's Arctic nuclear free.
There are 169 nuclear free zones in Canada as of June, 1987. Even in my own constituency, cities like Prince Rupert, Terrace, Kitimat, Smithers are nuclear free. Many others are trying to become nuclear free such as the Queen Charlotte Islands and other areas of the Pacific northwest. Major cities, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Regina, Toronto, Montreal, Bathurst, Lunenburg, cities and regional districts representing 59 per cent of Canadians now live in self-declared nuclear weapons free zones. The entire Province of Manitoba has recently passed a resolution before it making Manitoba a nuclear weapons free zone.
My Bill attempts to expand the zones, such as Vancouver where, for example, U.S. nuclear vessels tie up in the downtown area. That city and its councillors have declared all within their jurisdiction nuclear weapons free, but often at the
October 20, 1987

end of a rope at times rest vessels regularly armed with nuclear weapons in the middle of one of Canada's major cities.
The UN has long supported the establishment of nuclear weapons free zones as a means to bring about balanced verifiable disarmament. In 1978, the UN declared in its final report on disarmament:
The establishment of nuclear weapons free zone on the basis of arrangements arrived at among states in the region concerned constitutes an important disarmament initiative. The process of establishing such zones should be encouraged with the ultimate objective of achieving a world free of nuclear weapons.
Canada has internationally supported nuclear weapons free zones in the international theatre in 1978 and 1982. However, both Liberal and Conservative Governments have preached internationally but hidden from the issue here at home. The present war in the Persian Gulf surely reveals the importance of installing stronger mechanisms to achieve peace and to provide for nuclear weapons disarmament. The most recent silk worm missile attack of recent days against vessels carrying the American flag in Kuwaiti waters and even yesterday's bombing of Iranian oil platforms reveal the escalation in that zone.
Probably a lot of people in this House and in the country realize that over one million Iranian and Iraqi soldiers and citizens have already perished in the few short years of that conflict. Without strong leadership on the peace front this war will spread like cancer with real potential for a nuclear response.
The preposterous arguments trotted forward by the Government when this matter has been raised in the past must be taken head on. I would like to quote from one of the more recent debates where the central argument coming from the government benches is that if Canada adopted a nuclear weapons free zone resolution policy for all of Canadian territory, our obligations to our allies would be diminished. In fact, the former Minister of National Defence, the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), on August 31, 1987, as found on page 8630 of the Commons Debates, said in relation to the excellent motion by my friend, the Hon. Member for the Beaches (Mr. Young)
It would be foolhardy and dangerous for Canada to pass such a resolution.
I think we have to spend a moment and think here. We have the Secretary of State for External Affairs going to the UN and various functions around the world pushing and calling for other states to declare themselves nuclear weapons free zones, fighting for treaties for the sea bed and other areas of the globe, demanding that they declare themselves nuclear weapons free, but the key work to be done at home is put back on the shelf. Yet remarks totally unrelated to the motion and totally without any substantive logical argument are left on the record saying it would be foolhardy and dangerous to pass such a resolution. That flies in the face of two-thirds of Canada's population who have already, through various forms
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
of referenda and the electoral process, declared their immediate areas, be they a city, a town, a regional district or a province, nuclear weapons free.
Canada is nuclear weapons free in the Canadian military sense. But we are linked to weapons production, and by allowing particular U.S. vessels and aircraft to use our territory for transit of these weapons we are drawn further and further into the potential for either accident or conflict.
The NATO argument is constantly trotted out, but do we hear a peep from the same government back-benchers and cabinet members about Canada withdrawing from our historic commitment to provide troops to Norway? Nothing. No major speeches are given across the country by government Members about withdrawing from that sole responsibility in NATO. They point to the New Democrats and say "Oh, they want to withdraw from NATO." What hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker. The Government has already withdrawn our key commitments and has done nothing about the threats to our sovereignty and security in the Arctic. I want to spend a few moments on that.
The Government promised, it is going on years, that there was going to be a Polar 8 ice-breaker to provide the kind of sovereignty and security so dearly required in the Canadian Arctic. I responded to the Secretary of State for External Affairs following the voyage of the Polar Sea, unasked and unwanted through Canadian territory. The Government at that time promised it was going to build the largest ice-breaker in the world. Perhaps it would be built in Vancouver, certainly on the West Coast. I suppose that is being held back for an election promise and then another one years down the road. There is something more dire in the consequences of what the Government is doing.
What we see on the international stage is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) pursuing with vigour issues like apartheid, for which 1 congratulate him. Also we hear speeches given by Secretaries of State past and present on the need for nuclear weapons free zones and treaties around the world. What we should have on behalf of Canadians in a serious way is a declaration of the Arctic, all of the Arctic as a nuclear weapons and technology free zone. But there is no movement on that.
Instead what is the Government doing? It is proposing to acquire from France, Britain or somewhere outside of Canada, nuclear submarines. For what purpose? Not to be armed to go under the Canadian ice, to go into the Canadian North, but simply to go under the ice and monitor for surveillance purposes, to ping either American or Soviet or other submarines that we know have been lurking and operating unasked, unwanted and contrary to Canadian sovereignty within our territory.
Those who have taken a look at the implications of that policy realize quite quickly that the alternatives are far better in the interests of Canada in sovereignty and security as suggested at a meeting that I attended with people far more knowledgeable than I on military matters, security and

October 20, 1987
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
sovereignty. We have the technology, in hardware, software and computer submarine monitoring devices, to place the kinds of monitoring devices that we should have had long ago in the Canadian Arctic. We have the technology to monitor the movements of any vessels in, at, near, under or around our territory in the far North. Those are the kinds of technologies that should be implemented now, even before the construction of the Polar 8, so that we will have accurate, ongoing data for the preservation of both Canadian security and of Canadian sovereignty in the area.
Rather than that, what is the Government doing? We have not heard a peep about pursuing a resolution for Canada on a nuclear weapons free zone in the Arctic, not a peep about how to move accurately and properly forward to preserve our internationally recognized legal rights in the Arctic so that if we ever have to go to the International World Court in the Hague to put our case forward for Canadian sovereignty and security, we will have the kind of accurate and formidable legal data that we should have to win such a case.
When I was debating with the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the voyage of the Polar Sea, I was listening to what the Minister had to say about how we have come to secure sovereignty in the eyes of the world throughout all of the Arctic Archipelago, throughout all of that enormous mass of land, ice and water. This Government of all Governments placed sovereignty on the backs of the Inuit people. It said that the presence for thousands and tens of thousands of years on the ice, on the land and on the water in the High Arctic, in the Canadian North, was the root at international law for our sovereignty and security on this continent in the eyes of the world. Yet the same Government has taken no substantive movement on the comprehensive or specific claims of the Inuit or of the Dene, the Metis, the Yukon Indians, the Nishga, the Haida or any other aboriginal groups in Canada.
It is truly a preposterous state of affairs when the Government secures in the eyes of the world sovereignty and security on the backs of the Inuit but takes no steps, within the context of Canada's Constitution, which recognizes and affirms aboriginal title and rights, to give them the same kind of recognition that it provides to any forest company, any mining company, any corporate entity or anyone else.
One must spend a moment reflecting on the enormity of the psychological pressure on people of all generations who reflect at any time in their lives on the implications of nuclear weaponry and the possibility of a nuclear holocaust. Just think for a moment, the cost of one Canadian tank, usually constructed outside of Canada for military purposes, would pay for 520 classrooms for 15,000 children anywhere in the Third World. The cost of one nuclear submarine would pay for the education of 16 million children in the Third World for an entire year.
There are 50,000 plus nuclear weapons in the world now. How can an individual in Canadian society or elsewhere in the world confront that? How can people logically find a way to deal with that directly and to search internally and externally for peace? It is only through individual action and, as a starting point, declarations of nuclear weapons free zones.
The $800 billion that was spent in 1987-and it is expected to be $900 billion in the coming year-on world military expenditures amounts to $1.5 million per minute. How can intelligent, understanding people in Canada or elsewhere stand idly by knowing that every single day, thousands of children in the Third World are dying of malnutrition? If even a small amount of the money going into military hardware was diverted for disease control and for providing food and education, we would have a far better and a far more peaceful world for everyone to live in.
Along with huge and growing trade deficits and debts, we have now seen the U.S. economy begin to turn upside down. Every $1 billion dollars spent on the U.S. military creates
28,000	jobs in the United States. If that were spent in the transportation industry, it would create 32,000 jobs. If it were spent on goods and services, it would be 57,000 jobs or 71,000 jobs even in Canada or the United States if spent on education.
The jobs argument about the nuclear weapons industry is often self-serving drivel. Anyone who can understand the exorbitant costs of these expenditures on regional economies has to be saddened.
This debate must be an affirmation that Canada wants to influence national and international behaviour and nuclear policy. The world can return to peace and stability but only through leadership and the pursuit of peace.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR WEAPONS FREE ZONE ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to talk about nuclear disarmament and about the suggestion made in Bill C-214 which is before us and whose purpose is to establish a nuclear-free zone in Canada.

I have to say at the outset that I have a great deal of sympathy for the position put forward by my friend who is a member of the NDP. Obviously we share with him all the concerns that he has expressed, but the question surely before the House-

-the question which Hon. Members must examine is as follows: First, is this legislative measure truly realistic? Will such a unilateral declaration as that advocated by my friend lead to unmistakably concrete results with respect to nuclear disarmament, and will such an approach prove to be a worthwhile contribution to nuclear disarmament?
October 20, 1987



I suggest that notwithstanding the sympathy and support which I wish to offer to the spirit of this proposal, it does not meet those tests. I do not believe that a unilateral declaration of a nuclear weapons free zone as proposed is realistic. Second,
I do not believe it would be effective. Consequently, 1 do not think it would make a significant contribution to reducing or eliminating the threat of nuclear war on this planet.
That being said, 1 want to draw the attention of the House and of my hon. friend to the position of my own Party, the Liberal Party, as expressed at the November 1986 convention in a resolution which went specifically to this point. It was a resolution referred to, I believe, during an earlier debate in this House on the same subject, a resolution put forward by the association represented by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). A number of points were raised in that resolution but specifically it resolved that the Liberal Party of Canada move immediately to adopt a more imaginative and rigorous arms control policy which would include making Canada a nuclear weapons free zone.
1 want to emphasize at the outset that the Party to which I belong has taken that position, but as our Leader has carefully explained on numerous occasions, that must be done within the context of our international treaty obligations, specifically our obligations to NATO.
Let me say a word on definitions. What is a nuclear weapons free zone? There are many who define it in different ways, but Project Ploughshares, for example, tells us that in its view, it is a defined geographic area within which the possession, deployment, storage, transit, manufacture, testing or other support of nuclear weapons and nuclear weapons systems is prohibited.
I must say that Bill C-214 certainly seems compatible with that definition. In fact, I suggest it goes even further.
As the sponsor of the Bill pointed out, there are such nuclear weapons free zones established by treaty in four areas, namely the sea bed, outer space, Antarctica, and Latin America. In 1985, a zone was also set up in the South Pacific, but it is interesting to note that there the transit of nuclear weapons is specifically provided for. I gather that that zone was designed primarily to address the problem of nuclear testing. Indeed, the Nordic countries, Denmark, Norway and Iceland, have since 1958, I believe, tried to establish a nuclear weapons free zone in their area, so far without success. Similarly, some of the Balkan states have been trying to do this since 1959, specifically Greece, Romania, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and Turkey. Those are examples of either nuclear weapons free zones established by treaty or attempts to do so.
There are also examples of unilateral declarations, such as the proposal we have before us. Specifically, we have the example of New Zealand. You will recall that the U.S.
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
response to New Zealand's position was to remove protection and apply trade sanctions.

So the question is this, Mr. Speaker: Would a unilateral declaration on Canada being a nuclear-free zone be consistent with our NATO commitments? There are many who say yes, like Project Ploughshares whose NATO definition 1 have just referred to. But there are others who say no.
Mr. Speaker, I will refrain from elaborating on the legality of such a unilateral declaration, that is within the scope of our multilateral obligations, but will this kind of gesture help achieve the goals mentioned by the NDP spokesman?

As I said before, I do not think that a unilateral declaration would meet the objectives I described at the outset which surely must be the objectives of my friend from the NDP.
That being said, there is no need to be negative when faced with this proposal. There is no need to be negative with respect to the concept of a nuclear weapons free zone for Canada. After all, as the Hon. Member pointed out, we do not have and have not had nuclear weapons ourselves for some years as a matter of policy. Surely in itself that is a statement that others should not have them either.
There is no need to review the unthinkable consequences of any kind of nuclear confrontation on this planet. The question is: Would a unilateral declaration contribute? Or would it not, on the contrary, tend to remove Canada from nuclear policy decisions at the tables of NATO? Might it not compromise our ability to influence our allies on arms control? In addition, could we enforce it? Obviously we could not. Therefore it is not practical, it is not effective, and does not meet that test which 1 set at the outset.
What would? Obviously a negotiated multilateral nuclear weapons free zone to which Canada could be a party and in which territory of Canada could be involved is of course a realistic alternative. The Arctic is a logical place to begin.
I realize my time is short but I cannot help but mention the statement made by General Secretary Gorbachev in his recent visit to Murmansk on October 6 when he entertained the possibility of a negotiated nuclear weapons free zone in the Arctic. It had been my intention to read rather extensively from his comments because I think they are quite enlightening and should make us optimistic about the possibilities of demilitarization, if one could use that term, of the Arctic area.
He makes specific reference to the nuclear weapons free zone and perhaps concessions that might be made with respect to the Soviet arms currently situated in the Kola Peninsula. I know there is a certain amount of skepticism that one could effectively have a nuclear weapons free zone in the Arctic given the present significance of the Kola Peninsula for Soviet military purposes. Nonetheless, why not give it a chance? Why not find out? Who could object to a verifiable, enforceable

October 20, 1987
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
nuclear weapons free zone established by treaty to which the superpowers would be parties? That would be an effective way of making a significant contribution to nuclear disarmament. Surely that is the direction in which we should be moving.
In closing, the proposal in Bill C-214 is not realistic. It will not make a significant contribution to nuclear disarmament. However, the concept of a nuclear weapons free zone within the parameters 1 have described is something that indeed some day we may attain. That day may be sooner rather than later.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR WEAPONS FREE ZONE ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill reflects a concern that, as the Government is well aware, is on the minds of many Canadians. I refer to the role of nuclear weapons in preserving collective security and Canada's own responsibilities in that regard. Given the awesome destructive power of nuclear weapons, it is understandable that Canadians who reflect seriously on national and international security issues should be especially attentive to their Government's policies in this area.
First of all, I would like to emphasize that Canadian policy and practice are in many respects already in conformity with the provisions of Bill C-214. Canada does not possess nuclear weapons.
In normal peacetime conditions, no nuclear weapons are deployed, tested or constructed within Canada nor transported through Canada. Nor could such nuclear-weapons related activities occur on Canadian territory or under Canadian jurisdiction without the express consent of the Canadian Government.
I would remind the House that Canada's situation in this regard is very different from that of a number of our NATO allies who accept the stationing of nuclear weapons on their territory. As for Canadian exports, it is firm Canadian policy that all exports of nuclear material, equipment and technology shall be for peaceful, non-explosive purposes only.
This policy is strictly implemented through bilateral agreements and with the cooperation of the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to make it clear that the Government is in principle sympathetic to the broad concept of nuclear-weapon-free zones until such time as the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, which Canada strongly supports, achieves close to universal international adherence. Meanwhile, the establishment of such zones can make a contribution to the objective of preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. However, to be effective a nuclear-weapon-free zone must in our judgement fully meet the following criteria: apply to a well-defined region; have the support of the countries of the region; and, most importantly, promote regional and international stability.
From what 1 have said so far, Mr. Speaker, it should be apparent that the Government's approach is a pragmatic one. Our central concern is to ensure that in current and foreseeable circumstances our policies contribute to national security and international stability.
Canada's national security policy is based on the twin pillars of collective defence and arms control and disarmament. This Government's commitment to collective defence is exemplified in Canada's membership in NATO and NORAD. The primary role of the Alliance is to safeguard the security of member nations by deterring aggression. This Government believes, as do other NATO Governments, that the nuclear deterrence strategy of the Alliance has been a critically important element in maintaining peace in the East-West context for over 40 years. Canada has voluntarily shouldered the obligation to contribute to the capability of the Alliance to implement its strategy of deterrence. As I have mentioned, this has involved a less onerous burden for us than for several other Alliance members who have accepted the deployment of nuclear weapons on their territory. It would neither be consistent with our Alliance membership, nor with our own security interest, for Canada as a matter of principle to attempt to dissociate itself from any or all aspects of the nuclear deterrence strategy. This will remain an essential element of our collective defence until there is much greater progress in reducing levels of armaments, particularly strategic nuclear weapons, and in building a more secure world.
The second central pillar of our national security policy is arms control and disarmament. The Canadian Government, like other Alliance members, recognizes the desirability of moving toward reduced reliance on nuclear weapons. The fact that the USA and USSR are close to successfully concluding an agreement that will totally eliminate the whole category of intermediate-range nuclear weapons on a global basis is a significant milestone in the arms control process. These negotiations began as a result of an Alliance initiative. The progress in the negotiations has in no small measure been due to the ability of the Alliance to maintain a consistent, coordinated approach. The Alliance is similarly providing strong support for the efforts of the two superpowers to negotiate major reductions in their strategic nuclear arsenals. As we move toward a less nuclear world, the conventional balance of forces gains in importance. In this area too. Alliance members are coordinating their efforts to bring about negotiations with the objective of maintaining security through balanced reductions of armaments.
Canada has been able to make a serious and constructive input to these important arms control negotiating efforts, in which we have a direct interest, because of our presence at the table as an Alliance member. Without that membership card, Canada would be relegated to the spectators' gallery. Even in multilateral arms control forums, much of Canada's credibility and capacity for influence derives from our Alliance membership, which signals to others our level of knowledge about and direct involvement in the activities of key deliberative forums.
October 20, 1987

To the extent that we decline to assume our share of the collective defence burden, Canada's ability to influence events as an Alliance member would be diminished.
The question must be asked, Mr. Speaker, what would really be achieved by passing this Bill?
In many respects, as 1 have noted, nothing would change. Canada would remain a country without nuclear weapons and with no direct involvement in the manufacture and maintenance of nuclear arsenals. However, by signalling a righteous desire to dissociate ourselves from key aspects of the collective defence strategy of the Alliance, Canada's credibility and influence with our traditional European partners, not to mention the United States, would be significantly diminished. Our own security would certainly not be enhanced and could in fact be compromised. It would, in sum, be a worse than futile gesture which ignores the realities of today's interdependent world. This interdependence is just as real in the area of national security as in other areas.
Finally, this Bill provides that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should request the United Nations to hold a world referendum on nuclear disarmament. Mr. Speaker, in resurrecting this old chestnut, the Honourable Member is not helping to advance the arms control and disarmament process. Although a global expression in favour of nuclear disarmament would be fine in itself, it would not be a substitute for the negotiation of effective international arms control agreements. The call for a referendum fails to recognize that meaningful progress in reducing levels of nuclear weapons must be the product of negotiations among governments. There are no short-cuts or substitutes for the negotiating process.
Even if such a referendum were to be held, it is not clear how the results should be interpreted in view of the global diversity of political systems and approaches to freedom of expression.
Furthermore, practical considerations, such as the enormous expenses associated with such an undertaking at a time when the United Nations is attempting to avert financial crisis, would present a serious constraint.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, when comparing the uncertain benefits with the staggering costs, the utility of such a referendum is highly doubtful. Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons, 1 would strongly urge my colleagues on both sides of this House to vote against Bill C-214.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NUCLEAR WEAPONS FREE ZONE ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-214, an Act to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone. This Bill deals with a very fundamental issue to which no Canadian is indifferent, which is the role of nuclear deterrence in Canada's defence and security and in maintaining peace.
Canada has no nuclear arms and does not intend to purchase any. It has signed treaties guaranteeing the non-proliferation and prohibition of nuclear testing; furthermore, unlike most of
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
its allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, NATO, it neither stores nor deploys nuclear arms on its territory. According to the terms of the Bill, Canada is technically a nuclear weapons free zone in peace time. However, because of its geographic location, Canada must live with the threat of a nuclear holocaust which, in a conflict between the two superpowers, would make short thrift of neutrality and spare no one. There are only two ways to avert this threat: by maintaining a credible force to deter potential aggressors and through negotiation.
Canadians know that strategic deterrence is provided under NATO's collective security plan, and that we, for our defence, have to count on the nuclear forces of our allies. Today, the mutual deterrence system is effective and stable. Despite some of the worst crises, it has given us more than forty years of peace, and the Government believes this should continue. In this perspective, the Canadian Government's priority is not to create nuclear weapons free zones but to maintain peace zones.
As part of this common effort, since we count on our allies and they count on us to deter a potential adversary, we are in favour of developing and maintaining nuclear forces with the potential for survival that is necessary for an effective and credible deterrence system.
So, Mr. Speaker, even if Canada does not have and does not deploy nuclear arms, it contributes to strategic dissuasion.
Our role and our mandate are clear and have their roots in our geography and history. We must continue to ensure the aerospatial defence of North America, which we are doing through our defence effort and our association with NORAD. We must protect NATO strategic forces by forbidding access to our air space, our territory and our territorial waters to any potential aggressor. And Mr. Speaker, this is the real purpose of the defence program of the Government. Last, we must put our territory and our facilities to the disposal of our allies if required.
We fulfill those obligations and those collective security tasks in the full respect of our sovereignty and our integrity. In peace time we cooperate in the training and development of the dissuasion force. In time of crisis, Canada could authorize the strategic force components to fly over its territory and use its facilities.
It is essential and in keeping with our policy and our commitments that our air space and fire ranges continue to be used for the testing and development of non-armed components, that our Armed Forces train with the Atlantic Alliance Forces and that the dissuasion force ships visit our harbours.
It is not a threat for our country but it is part and parcel of its security and its commitment to peace.
A commitment to peace which results in a sustained negociation effort toward arms control and disarmament. These negotiations are unprecedented because of their duration and intensity, and they are contributing to the dialogue between East and West. Our presence at these

October 20, 1987
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
negotiations and our ability to influence how they are carried out and what results are achieved can also be attributed to our membership in the Atlantic Alliance. Because of our defence effort and of our role in collective defence, Canada is a valid and credible participant which can and does take certain initiatives.
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that the best way for us to contribute to world peace and security would be to break away from NATO or to weaken the deterrent strength of the Alliance. As abhorrent as might seem the use of nuclear weapons to ensure our defence, their presence is essential to counterbalance the Soviet arsenals. To renounce to these weapons would be a violation of our commitments, but it would also disturb the balance which is essential to maintain world peace.
Mr. Speaker, when I read the proposal of the socialist Member, I am tempted to ask him certain questions about his philosophy for peace and the general ideas of his socialist party for the protection of our western civilization, North America and Canada. 1 would like to know what his party would suggest as an alternative solution if Canada were to break off its association with NATO as his socialist colleagues have proposed. I find it strange that Canada would be asked to disassociate itself from a very credible international defence force while other members of the same party have asked that war be waged in certain countries. It is true that, since this request was officially made by certain socialist members, their leader decided to demote to the rear rows those who had been responsible for these initiatives, which were to say the least bellicose on the part of people who would like to eliminate nuclear weapons.
It would be better if the members of the socialist party agreed on a way to protect Canadians. If they prefer the protection of the Soviet Union, they should not be living in this country. They should move elsewhere, along with their colleagues. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I oppose the motion of the socialist member because I am happy to live in a free country in North America where citizens are free and prosperous, and it is in fact because of this prosperity that these socialists can become parasites of our western civilization.

But I would like to stress, Mr. Speaker, that our Government is open in principle to the general concept of nuclear weapons free zones. The establishment of such zones may be a
October 20, 1987

positive factor when most countries of a region agree to it and when it can promote regional and international stability.
Canada supported several U.N. resolutions calling for the creation of nuclear weapons free zones. This is what 1 wanted to say when I was taking notes earlier. There is nothing new in the Hon. Member's proposal.

Mr. Speaker, all of what 1 just said shows that the approach chosen by the Governement is obviously one of pragmatism. We want to make sure that, in the present and foreseeable circumstances, our policies will contribute to our national security and to international stability.
Our collective defence is one of the main tenets in the national security policy of this Government as is evidenced by our participation in NATO and NORAD, which 1 mentioned a moment ago.
The first role of the Alliance is to preserve the security of member nations by deterring every form of aggression. Our Government, like all others within NATO, is convinced that the strategy of nuclear deterrence has played, for the last 40 years, a very important role in maintaining peace between East and West. Canada, Mr. Speaker, has agreed on its own free will to contribute to the Alliance and its capacity to enforce its strategy of deterrence even though, as 1 mentioned, our burden has been lighter than the one of other members.
It would not make sense for Canada, considering that we are a member of the Alliance and that we have specific security interests, to dissociate itself from some or all aspects of the strategy of nuclear deterrence, as is the desire of our colleagues opposite.
As it happens, this strategy is still one of the key factors of our collective defence effort until such time as we make significant progress towards arms control. Arms control and disarmament make up the second mainstay of our national security policy. Echoing the position taken by other NATO member countries, the Canadian Government acknowledges that decreasing dependence on nuclear weapons is a commendable objective.

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) on his question and on the remarks he has made. At the outset, I would agree with him that the socialist Party certainly is a Party of apostles of fear. They fear any change. They look for the status quo. They can build only on the past and what the past has shown them. Because they think that way, they cannot anticipate any new changes which might produce something new or some new patterns.
People wonder why a free trade deal is good for Canada. The answer is very simple. It will create business for Canada and, if it creates business, it will create jobs for Canadians.
As my friend knows, the Economic Council of Canada has suggested that there might be a quarter or a third of a million jobs created as a result of this free trade deal. Why and how can we imagine that that would happen? It is very simple. It is a matter of numbers. Canada is made up of 25 million people. The United States has 10 times that many. It is the largest single market in the world.
Why should Canada not have free access to the single largest market? At present, Canadian companies service 25 million people. Why should they not service 275 million people? The simple mathematics are that if they can manufacture for 275 million people rather than for 25 million people,
they can increase the size of their plants, their companies, their assembly lines.
This means that to do that they will have to hire people. If they can manufacture tires, generators, light bulbs, or any other commodity to service 275 million people, including the entire U.S. market, why should they not be able to do that?
The fact is that there is no such thing as a status quo in the world market. The unions and the socialists may want to stay where we are, but there is no staying where we are because the rest of the world is going to compete, and somebody is going to get that quarter of a billion people for a market. It may as well be Canadians rather than the rest of the world.
Why should not Canadian business people take advantage of that large market? Why should not consumers benefit from the added variety of product which would be available to them?
I want to add to my comments a quotation from Peter Cook in an edition of The Globe and Mail of last week headlined "Protecting Canada from the worst of enemies". There are those who say that we will be swallowed up by the United States. Let me read what Peter Cook says:
The critics, in their negative way, contend that getting closer to the United States is a desperately dangerous exercise. It has not been dangerous for Ireland with Britain, or Denmark with West Germany, or New Zealand with Australia. And, as of this moment, tiny countries such as Malta and Cyprus arc clamouring to get inside the EC.
To swallow the arguments of the "antis" is to say that what is good for the rest of the world is somehow bad for Canada.
All of the little countries that are in marketing systems like this have benefited. Even though they are small countries next to large countries, they have benefited. Why should Canada not get the benefit of having a large market at its disposal and let Canadian business thrive?

Mr. Speaker, on August 20, 1987 I posed a question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with regard to the profits of drug manufacturing companies. In my question I noted that from 1968 to 1982 pharmaceutical companies in Canada made some very healthy and substantial profits. This was recently confirmed in the report which was made available by Dr. Eastman, who studied the pharmaceutical industry. In particular, he looked at the profit margins of companies operating as a result of the passage of amendments to the Patent Act, namely, compulsory licensing.
It was very clear from the evidence used by Dr. Eastman that those companies, notwithstanding their serious objections to compulsory licensing, made substantial profits. In fact, their profits were so substantial that they led the manufacturing sector in terms of percentage. At the present time, the profits
October 20, 1987

are higher than those in Japan, Germany, Britain, France and Switzerland. What is perhaps even more appalling with regard to Bill C-22 is that not only will it provide additional profit to companies that are already profitable, but it will take much needed money from those Canadians who need it most.
It should be very clear that who will be paying the higher drug prices in this country will be the provincial Governments-yes, provincial Governments right across this land- and individuals who are not covered by drug programs. Inevitably this comes to the Canadian consumer who will pay the lion's share of the additional profits which will go to multinational corporations as a result of the passage of Bill C-22.
It should be understood that no one argues against profits or the private sector making a reasonable profit. No one should argue against that. I think there is an argument to be made that if one receives reasonable profits and those profits are extended without any guarantees for research and development, for protection of the Canadian consumer and to create jobs, and guarantees of jobs then bad public policy is contained in Bill C-22.
It was adduced at committee, debated in the House and it is very clear that multinational corporations and the national Conservative Government believe strongly in their case that new jobs will be created and thousands upon thousands of new dollars will be funneled into research and development in our pharmaceutical industry. Surely the Government ought to ask those companies in whom it is placing its faith to put up a performance bond as a bare minimum in order to meet the objectives which it has set. Unfortunately, the Government has chosen another route, which is not to seek public guarantees for research and development, for the protection of the Canadian consumer or to create thousands of new jobs. We all hope that would result from any piece of legislation which would be passed by this Parliament.
I have grave difficulties with the answers that we have been receiving to date, and even in Oral Question Period there have been no guarantees whatsoever. It all comes back to profits and who is paying for those profits for multinational corporations. It is done through a number of auspices including provincial Governments and drug plans of another sort, but it is the Canadian consumer who will pay more for drugs.
I think that it is a shame. In fact, six provincial Governments have expressed serious reservations about Bill C-22. Thousands upon thousands of Canadians and organizations of senior citizens and veterans and even the United Church have opposed Bill C-22 for the very serious effects it will have on Canadians, and particularly for the costs that it will impose on Canadians, costs which will drive up the profits of a select few when many, many Canadians do not have the necessary finances to pay for their drugs.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-REPORT ON BATTERED WOMEN-LACK OF SPACE IN TRANSITION HOUSES
STATUS OF WOMEN-REPORT ON BATTERED WOMEN-LACK OF SPACE IN TRANSITION HOUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a lawyer who has practised a good deal of family law I have listened to many, many stories about family violence and wife abuse, including a number involving attempted murder. When I had the opportunity to read the report sponsored by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women written by a sociologist, Linda McCloud, entitled "Battered but not Beaten: Preventing Wife Battering in Canada", the story it told did not come as something new out of the blue. In fact, I served for some six years as a member of the Community and Social Services Committee in Metropolitan Toronto, and we dealt with the establishment of something called the Domestic Response Team. As a result of the problems flowing from family violence and wife beating, we established on an experimental basis a team approach in responding to such calls. It was made up of two police officers and a social worker. The police officers of course went to deal with the violence and the social worker went to deal with the counselling aspect. That program grew from an experimental approach into one that now covers all of Metropolitan Toronto.
As a result of that experience and my experiences as a lawyer, I certainly am familiar with the problems set out in that report. At the same time, that has not prevented me from being shocked by the fact that the report spells out that there is something like a million women each year who suffer from family violence and abuse. It has not prevented me from being shocked by specific examples set out in that report or by the fact there is such a lack of shelter for women in situations of this sort.
I do not know whether you or the Parliamentary Secretary have ever had the opportunity to visit a shelter or hostel. I have not had the opportunity to visit one for women but I have had the opportunity to visit one for men. In fact, I headed a task force that looked into one of the major men's hostels in Metropolitan Toronto, Seaton House, a few years ago. We found that while these facilities provided clean surroundings, hot meals, hot showers and other things which are obviously welcome to anyone in need, at the same time they are not the sort of places that you and I or our families would enjoy spending a night or week in. They are a communal-type of living experience where everyone there, including you, has problems, some more severe than others. As a result, although a person who has suffered from family violence obviously is looking for some shelter in some transition house, these kinds of facilities are not the kind that you and I would really want to go to, notwithstanding the fact we may need to if we do not have a family or friends that will take us in.
If a woman and her children are victims of family violence and have to go to a facility like this, that is bad enough. However, according to the report, one of every two women who attempt to go to a shelter or transition house facility have to be turned away because there are not enough facilities available. That is more than just disturbing, it is extremely shocking, particularly in this International Year of Shelter for the Homeless.
In his answer to my question in the House, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) indicated that since the Government came to power in 1984 there has been a very substantial increase in the number of shelters available for women who have been abused. That is admirable. In fact, the Minister pointed out that of the approximately 265 shelters which now exist about 100 are cost-shared between the federal and provincial governments.
However, the Minister also said that there is some distance to go. It is obvious that when one out of two women is turned away from a shelter there is some distance to go. Canadians are looking to the Government for word that we will close this distance and eliminate it altogether.
I know that the Parliamentary Secretary is a very humane man and has a social conscience as has his cousin, Mr. Colin Friesen, who is a neighbour of mine. He also has a very strong social conscience and is looking to the Parliamentary Secretary for an answer tonight as am I and other Canadians. We are looking for some concrete evidence that the Government intends to close this gap very quickly to ensure that shelters are available for women and families in need of them.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank my colleague for raising this matter which weighs on the hearts and minds of many Canadians. It first developed national prominence when it was brought to the attention of the House by our colleague, the Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) of New Brunswick during Private Members' Hour. It went to committee and a report on battered women was tabled in the House on the subject. I want to compliment my friend, the Member for York East (Mr. Redway), for the work he is doing in sensitizing the public to this issue as well as complimenting our colleague from York-Sunbury who raised the issue five or six years ago for the same purpose.
This subject is recognized by an increasing number of people. It is a societal issue. Transition homes are needed to an increasing degree to help these people.
The matter of providing financial support, shelter, and social services to battered women and their children falls under the jurisdiction of the individual provinces and the territories. The federal Government, through the Canada Assistance Plan, assists Canadians by sharing in costs to provinces and territories for providing financial assistance and social services to persons who meet the eligibility requirements. The province,
October 20, 1987

on the other hand, assumes responsibility for determining eligibility and deciding on the amount or type and extent of social services that are to be provided within the province or territory.
The Canada Assistance Plan shares in the costs incurred by provinces and municipalities for operating transition homes for battered women and their children. The care and social services provided to the residents are shared as assistance costs on behalf of persons in need based on the applications of the needs test. Federal funding is not limited to any predetermined amount and is available to all provinces and territories.
In 1987 CAP shared on behalf of women in need and their children in approximately 130 transition and crisis centres across the country. It is estimated that 265 centres currently provide emergency shelter to women and their children. In addition, the plan provided sharing in provincial costs for counselling, day care, rehabilitation and a wide range of other social services benefiting victims of violence.
Some time ago, Canada Assistance Plan policy was changed to accept the use of an abbreviated needs test in emergency situations for determining eligibility in relation to short term care. This gives provinces and territories the flexibility to simplify their admission policies and provide emergency shelter in crisis situations without losing cost sharing.
Adjournment Debate
It is also important to note that National Health and Welfare through the Family Violence Prevention Division, is concerned that a comprehensive approach to education and prevention of wife assault has to be firmly promoted. The Family Violence Prevention Division provides the necessary liaison and co-ordination of activities, clarifies issues and provides general information. This general information is provided mainly through the National Clearing House on Family Violence. Provincial involvement is necessary if the incidents of wife battering and violence in general within the family is to be reduced.
May 1 add, for my hon. friend, that if there are a million women who are battered each year, there are a million men who are sick and need treatment. Women need shelter and there is an increasing need for role modeling that is healthy, supportive and constructive within the family, and that will deal with this issue. While shelter is important and we must provide it for these distressed families, there must be a cure for these people who are sick and need to Find a different way of handling their problems rather than battering wives.
